chapters.title: The Living World
chapters.intro: These notes rebuild NCERT Class XI Chapter 1 from every concept tested in the question bank. Read them top to bottom and you should be able to answer all the chapter's MCQs. Each heading has a stable id so individual MCQs can later be linked to the exact section they test.

sections.heading: 1. What does 'living' mean?
sections.html:
The question “What is life?” hides two questions:

  • a technical question — what distinguishes the living from the non-living;
  • a philosophical question — what is the purpose of life.

As scientists we deal only with the technical question; the philosophical one (purpose of life) lies outside the scope of scientific inquiry. So biology defines life through a set of defining characteristics: growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation, consciousness/response to stimuli, and the ability to self-replicate, evolve and self-regulate while interacting with the environment.

Living organisms can be unexceptionally distinguished from non-living things by their ability to sense their surroundings and respond to stimuli (physical, chemical or biological) — this responsiveness, together with self-consciousness in humans, is the most defining attribute.

sections.heading: 1.1 Growth
sections.html:
Growth = irreversible increase in mass and in the number of cells. Its twin characteristics are (i) increase in mass and (ii) increase in number of cells.

  • In plants, growth by cell division continues throughout life (growth is said to be open).
  • In animals, growth by cell division occurs only up to a certain age.
  • In living organisms growth is from inside (intrinsic), by addition of material and cell division.
  • Non-living objects (mountains, boulders, sand mounds) can also “grow” — but only by accumulation of material on the surface (from outside). A dead body does not grow.

Because non-living things also increase in size, growth cannot be taken as a defining property of living organisms. In unicellular organisms (e.g. Amoeba, bacteria) growth — increase in number of cells — is synonymous with reproduction. In higher plants and animals, growth and reproduction are mutually exclusive events.

sections.heading: 1.2 Reproduction
sections.html:
Reproduction = production of progeny possessing features more or less similar to the parents. Modes seen in the living world include:

  • Budding — Hydra, yeast, and sponges.
  • Fragmentation — fungi, filamentous algae, and the protonema of mosses multiply by fragmentation.
  • Regeneration / true regeneration — Planaria regenerates a whole organism from a fragment.
  • In unicellular organisms, reproduction is synonymous with growth (cell division increases the number of individuals).

Reproduction is not an all-inclusive defining property, because many organisms do not reproduce (e.g. mules, sterile worker bees, infertile human couples) yet are clearly living. Hence reproduction alone cannot define life.

sections.heading: 1.3 Metabolism
sections.html:
Metabolism = the sum total of all the chemical reactions occurring in the body. It includes anabolism (build-up reactions) and catabolism (break-down reactions).

  • All living organisms — plants, animals, fungi and microbes — exhibit metabolism; it powers growth, development and functioning.
  • No non-living object exhibits metabolism. Metabolism is therefore a strong defining feature of life.
  • Metabolic reactions can be carried out outside the body in cell-free systems (e.g. in a test tube). Such an isolated reaction is a surrogate — it is neither living nor non-living.

sections.heading: 1.4 Cellular organisation & consciousness
sections.html:
Cellular organisation of the body is the defining feature of life forms. Properties at each level are the result of interactions among the lower-level components:

  • Properties of cellular organelles are not present in their molecular constituents but arise from interactions among them.
  • Properties of tissues arise from interactions among constituent cells (they are not present in the isolated cells).
  • Properties of organs arise from interactions among constituent tissues.

Consciousness / response to stimuli is the defining property of living organisms. All organisms — from prokaryotes to the most complex — sense and respond to environmental cues (light, water, temperature, other organisms, pollutants). Photoperiod affects reproduction in seasonal breeders, both plants and animals. All organisms handle chemicals entering their bodies. Humans are the only organism with self-consciousness (awareness of self). Thus living organisms are self-replicating, evolving, self-regulating interactive systems capable of responding to external stimuli.

sections.heading: 2. Diversity in the living world
sections.html:
The living world is enormously diverse. Wherever we look — a small area, a dense forest, an ocean, a desert, a cold mountain, a freshwater lake, or a hot spring — we find living organisms, many of them microscopic and invisible to the naked eye. Increasing the area of observation steadily increases the number and variety of organisms seen.

Each distinct kind of plant, animal or organism represents a species. The number and types of organisms present on Earth is called biodiversity. About 1.7–1.8 million species are currently known and described, and this number keeps increasing as new and old areas are explored — a large number of organisms still remain unknown.

sections.heading: 2.1 Need for naming — Nomenclature
sections.html:
Local (common/vernacular) names vary from place to place, even within one country, causing confusion. To allow biologists everywhere to refer to an organism by the same name, names are standardised — this process is called nomenclature.

Nomenclature is possible only when the organism has first been correctly described and identified (identification precedes naming). Scientific naming is governed by international codes:

  • ICBN — International Code for Botanical Nomenclature (for plants).
  • ICZN — International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (for animals).

Scientific names ensure each organism has one unique name not used for any other known organism, and that a proper description lets biologists worldwide arrive at the same name.

sections.heading: 2.2 Binomial nomenclature
sections.html:
Binomial nomenclature — a two-word naming system — was given by Carolus Linnaeus and is used by biologists all over the world because the two-word format is convenient. Linnaeus published it in Systema Naturae (and later Species Plantarum).

Each scientific name has two components: the generic name (genus) first, and the specific epithet (species) second. Universal rules of writing:

  • Biological names are generally in Latin or are Latinised, irrespective of where the organism comes from (Latin is a 'dead' language, so spellings do not change with time). Names can not be written in any other language.
  • When printed, names are in italics; when handwritten, the two words are underlined separately.
  • The genus begins with a capital letter; the specific epithet with a small letter.
  • The author's name, often abbreviated, is written after the specific epithet (e.g. Mangifera indica Linn., where Linn. = Linnaeus first described the species).

Scientific names to remember

  • Mango — Mangifera indica · Potato — Solanum tuberosum · Makoi/black nightshade — Solanum nigrum · Brinjal — Solanum melongena · Wheat — Triticum aestivum
  • Man — Homo sapiens · Housefly — Musca domestica · Lion — Panthera leo · Tiger — Panthera tigris · Leopard — Panthera pardus · Cat — Felis domesticus

sections.heading: 3. Classification, taxa & taxonomy
sections.html:
Classification is the process by which organisms are grouped into convenient categories based on easily observable characters (and on similarities and dissimilarities). These categories — e.g. 'Dogs', 'Mammals', 'Plants', 'Wheat' — are scientifically called taxa (singular: taxon). A taxon can indicate categories at very different levels (from a broad group like Plants to a narrow one like Wheat).

Taxonomy is the science of classifying organisms into taxa on the basis of their characteristics. Its four basic processes are: characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature. Modern taxonomic studies use external and internal structure, cell structure, development process and ecological information (not the commercial value of the organism). The earliest classifications were based on the uses of organisms (food, clothing, shelter).

sections.heading: 3.1 Taxonomy vs Systematics
sections.html:
Interest in the relationships among different kinds of organisms led to the branch called systematics. The word comes from the Latin systema (systematic arrangement of organisms); Linnaeus used Systema Naturae as the title of his work.

  • The scope of systematics was later enlarged to include identification, nomenclature and classification.
  • Unlike early utility-based taxonomy, systematics also takes into account the evolutionary relationships between organisms — giving it a broader scope than taxonomy alone.
  • Biosystematics classifies organisms on the basis of their evolutionary history, establishing phylogeny using data from many fields (anatomy, ecology, physiology, biochemistry, etc.).

sections.heading: 4. Taxonomic categories & hierarchy
sections.html:
Classification is not a single step but involves a hierarchy of steps, each step (rank) representing a category. All categories together form the taxonomic hierarchy, and each category — being a unit of classification — is called a taxon. Taxonomic categories are distinct biological entities, not merely morphological aggregates.

The seven obligate categories, from lowest to highest, are: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum/Division → Kingdom. (Figure 1.1 shows them in ascending order, starting with species.) Sub-categories (sub-genus, sub-species, etc.) were introduced for more precise placement.

Key rule: as we move from species up to kingdom, the number of common characteristics decreases, and it becomes more difficult to determine relationships among taxa at the same level. Members of a lower taxon share more characters than members of a higher taxon.

sections.heading: 4.1 Species
sections.html:
Species is the basic / lowest unit of classification — a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring (biological species concept, defined by Ernst Mayr, the 'Darwin of the 20th century'). All other categories are defined in relation to species. Closely related species are distinguished by distinct morphological differences.

Examples (the specific epithet is the species name): indica in Mangifera indica, tuberosum in Solanum tuberosum, leo in Panthera leo.

sections.heading: 4.2 Genus
sections.html:
A genus is an aggregate of closely related species — species that share more characters in common with one another than with species of other genera. A single genus may contain one or more species.

  • Solanum includes potato (S. tuberosum), brinjal (S. melongena) and makoi (S. nigrum).
  • Panthera includes lion (P. leo), leopard (P. pardus) and tiger (P. tigris); whereas the domestic cat is placed in genus Felis.

sections.heading: 4.3 Family
sections.html:
A family is a group of related genera and has still fewer similarities than genus and species. Plant families are characterised on the basis of both vegetative and reproductive (floral) features.

  • Plant family endings: -aceae. e.g. Solanaceae (genera Solanum, Petunia, Datura), Convolvulaceae, Poaceae, Anacardiaceae, Liliaceae.
  • Animal family endings: -idae. e.g. Felidae (genera Panthera, Felis), Canidae (dogs), Muscidae (housefly), Hominidae (man).
  • Cats → family Felidae; Dogs → family Canidae.

sections.heading: 4.4 Order
sections.html:
An order is a higher category that assembles families sharing a few similar characters; these characters are fewer than those shared by genera within a family. Orders are identified using aggregates of characters.

  • Plant order Polymoniales includes families Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae (grouped mainly on floral characters).
  • Animal order Carnivora includes families Felidae and Canidae (tiger, cat, dog).
  • Order Primata includes monkey, gorilla and gibbon; order Diptera includes the housefly.

sections.heading: 4.5 Class
sections.html: A class groups related orders. For example, class Mammalia contains orders Primata, Carnivora and others (so monkey, tiger and dog are all mammals but lie in different orders). The housefly belongs to class Insecta, whose members typically have three pairs of jointed legs in the thoracic region.

sections.heading: 4.6 Phylum / Division
sections.html:
Related classes are grouped into the next higher category: Phylum for animals and Division for plants (so the plant equivalent of an animal phylum is a division). The term phylum was given by Cuvier.

  • Phylum Chordata — animals with a notochord and a dorsal hollow neural (nerve) cord (e.g. fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals — including man). Arthropods, by contrast, have a ventral nerve cord.
  • Housefly belongs to phylum Arthropoda (an invertebrate).

sections.heading: 4.7 Kingdom
sections.html: Kingdom is the highest category in this hierarchy. All animals are placed in Kingdom Animalia and all plants (from various divisions) in Kingdom Plantae.

sections.heading: 5. Taxonomical aids
sections.html: Taxonomical aids are the techniques, procedures and stored information used for the identification, classification and study of organisms. The prime source of taxonomic study is the collection of actual specimens.

sections.heading: 5.1 Herbarium
sections.html: A herbarium is a store of dried, pressed and preserved plant specimens mounted on sheets, identified and arranged according to an accepted classification. The herbarium sheet label carries the scientific name, family, common/vernacular name, locality (place of collection), date of collection, collection number and the collector's name — but not the height of the plant. Herbaria serve as quick referral systems. The Indian Botanical Garden (IBG) is at Howrah.

sections.heading: 5.2 Botanical gardens
sections.html: Botanical gardens maintain collections of living plants for reference; each plant is labelled with its botanical name and family. They allow ex situ conservation of germplasm and hold collections of endemic and exotic species. Famous examples: Kew (England) and the National Botanical Research Institute (NBRI), Lucknow.

sections.heading: 5.3 Museums
sections.html: Museums have collections of preserved plant and animal specimens for study and reference. Animals are kept as preserved specimens in jars/containers (in preservative solutions), as dry insect collections after killing and pinning, or as stuffed/skeleton specimens for larger animals. (Insects are killed and pinned, not pressed.)

sections.heading: 5.4 Zoological parks
sections.html: Zoological parks (zoos) are places where wild animals are kept in protected conditions resembling their natural habitats, so we can study their food habits and behaviour and conserve them. The single-horned (Indian) rhinoceros is a natural inhabitant of Kaziranga National Park, Assam.

sections.heading: 5.5 Keys
sections.html: A key is an analytical aid for identification based on contrasting characters. Keys are dichotomous — at each step they offer two contrasting choices, and each pair of contrasting characters is called a couplet; each statement in a couplet is a lead. Separate keys are used for each taxonomic category. Keys are used in the preparation of flora, manuals and monographs.

sections.heading: 5.6 Flora, Manuals, Monographs & Catalogues
sections.html:
• Flora — contains the actual account of habitat and distribution of plants of a given area; provides an index to the plant species of that area.
  • Manuals — provide information for the identification of names of species found in an area.
  • Monographs — contain information on any one taxon (a single complete group).
  • Catalogue — a record/list used alongside the above.

Bentham and Hooker's Genera Plantarum is a classic monograph-style work providing keys for the identification of natural orders and genera.

sections.heading: 6. Why taxonomy matters
sections.html: Taxonomic studies of plants, animals and other organisms are useful in agriculture, forestry, industry and in knowing our bio-resources and their diversity — helping us identify useful and harmful organisms (but not fields such as astrology). The basics of taxonomy — identification, naming and classification — are universally governed by international codes, and every organism, by the binomial system, gets a two-word scientific name and occupies a definite position in the classification system. Despite ~1.7–1.8 million described organisms, a large number still remain unknown.

chapters.title: Biological Classification
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 2 rebuilt to cover every concept tested in the bank: the history of classification, Whittaker's Five Kingdom system, and the detailed biology of Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, plus the acellular entities — viruses, viroids, prions and lichens.

sections.heading: 1. History & need for classification
sections.html:
Early classification was driven by use. Aristotle was the first to attempt a more scientific basis, dividing plants into trees, shrubs and herbs and animals into those with red blood (RBC) and those without.

Two-kingdom system (Linnaeus) — Plantae and Animalia — was used long but was inadequate: it did not distinguish eukaryotes from prokaryotes, unicellular from multicellular, or photosynthetic (green algae) from non-photosynthetic (fungi). Characters such as cell structure, nature of cell wall, mode of nutrition, habitat, methods of reproduction and evolutionary relationships were later used to build better systems.

sections.heading: 2. Five Kingdom Classification (Whittaker, 1969)
sections.html:
R. H. Whittaker (1969) proposed the Five Kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. The main criteria were: cell structure (prokaryotic vs eukaryotic), body organisation, mode of nutrition (autotrophic / heterotrophic — absorptive or ingestive), reproduction and phylogenetic relationships.

Cell typeProkaryoticEukaryoticEukaryoticEukaryoticEukaryotic
Cell wallNon-cellulosic (polysaccharide + amino acid)Present in somePresent (chitin)Present (cellulose)Absent
Nuclear membraneAbsentPresentPresentPresentPresent
Body organisationCellularCellularMulticellular / loose tissueTissue / organTissue / organ / organ-system
NutritionAutotrophic & heterotrophicAutotrophic & heterotrophicHeterotrophic (saprophytic/parasitic)Autotrophic (photosynthetic)Heterotrophic (holozoic/saprophytic)

Limitation: each kingdom is still heterogeneous — e.g. Monera and Protista lump together very diverse organisms with/without cell walls and different nutrition. A separate Kingdom Fungi and the assembly of all prokaryotes in Monera were major improvements.

sections.heading: 3. Kingdom Monera (bacteria)
sections.html: All prokaryotes are placed in Monera. Bacteria are the most abundant micro-organisms, found almost everywhere. By shape: Coccus (spherical), Bacillus (rod), Vibrio (comma), Spirillum (spiral).

sections.heading: 3.1 Bacterial cell structure
sections.html:
• Cell wall — made of peptidoglycan; determines shape and Gram reaction (Gram +ve vs Gram −ve). Mycoplasma lack a cell wall (hence pleomorphic).
  • Glycocalyx — outer sticky layer; a thick tough one is a capsule, a loose one is a slime layer.
  • Flagella — for motility; fimbriae — small bristles that help attach to rocks/host tissue; pili — for conjugation.
  • Mesosomes — infoldings of the plasma membrane that perform respiration (mitochondria-like roles); aid cell wall formation, DNA replication and secretion.
  • Chromatophores — pigment-bearing membranous extensions in some photosynthetic bacteria/cyanobacteria.
  • A single circular nucleoid (no nuclear membrane), 70S ribosomes, and often extra-chromosomal plasmids.

sections.heading: 3.2 Bacterial nutrition & reproduction
sections.html:
Autotrophic bacteria are photosynthetic or chemosynthetic. Heterotrophic bacteria are the most abundant — important as decomposers, in curd/antibiotic/nitrogen-fixation, but some are pathogens.

Reproduction is mainly by binary fission; under stress they form spores. They also show a primitive DNA transfer (conjugation/transformation/transduction). The bacterial growth curve has four phases: lag → log (exponential) → stationary → decline.

sections.heading: 3.3 Archaebacteria
sections.html: Archaebacteria live in the most harsh habitats thanks to a different cell wall structure (branched-chain lipids in the membrane). Three groups: halophiles (extreme salt), thermoacidophiles (hot acidic springs, pH≈2), and methanogens — which live in the gut of ruminants and produce methane (biogas) from dung. Hyperthermophiles of acidic habitats span eubacteria and archaea.

sections.heading: 3.4 Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae)
sections.html: Cyanobacteria (= blue-green algae, BGA) are photosynthetic prokaryotes with chlorophyll a; they carry out oxygenic photosynthesis (e.g. Oscillatoria, Nostoc, Anabaena). Colonies are surrounded by a gelatinous sheath. Some fix atmospheric N₂ in specialised cells called heterocysts. Excess growth in polluted water causes algal blooms.

sections.heading: 3.5 Mycoplasma
sections.html: Mycoplasma are the smallest living cells known. They lack a cell wall (so are pleomorphic), can survive without oxygen, and many are pathogenic to plants and animals.

sections.heading: 4. Kingdom Protista
sections.html: All single-celled eukaryotes are placed in Protista — a kingdom that forms a link between plants, animals and fungi. Members are primarily aquatic. It unites organisms once placed in different kingdoms (e.g. Chlamydomonas/Chlorella with Paramoecium/Amoeba).

sections.heading: 4.1 Chrysophytes (diatoms & desmids)
sections.html: Include diatoms and golden algae (desmids). Cell walls form two overlapping siliceous shells that fit like a soap-box; the indestructible walls accumulate as diatomaceous earth. Diatoms are the chief producers in the oceans.

sections.heading: 4.2 Dinoflagellates
sections.html: Mostly marine and photosynthetic; appear yellow, green, brown, blue or red. Rapid multiplication of red dinoflagellates (e.g. Gonyaulax) causes a red tide; their toxins can kill fish. They have two flagella and stiff cellulose plates on the wall.

sections.heading: 4.3 Euglenoids
sections.html: Fresh-water organisms (e.g. Euglena) with a protein-rich flexible pellicle instead of a cell wall. They are photosynthetic autotrophs in sunlight but turn heterotrophic in its absence (mixotrophic) — a plant-animal link.

sections.heading: 4.4 Slime moulds
sections.html: Saprophytic protists. Under suitable conditions the body (plasmodium) grows large; under unfavourable conditions it forms fruiting bodies with spores that have true walls, are extremely resistant and survive for long periods.

sections.heading: 4.5 Protozoans
sections.html: All heterotrophic — predators or parasites, believed to be primitive relatives of animals. Four groups: Amoeboid (e.g. Amoeba, Entamoeba — uses pseudopodia; Amoeba has a contractile vacuole for osmoregulation), Flagellated (e.g. Trypanosoma), Ciliated (e.g. Paramoecium), and Sporozoans (e.g. Plasmodium).

sections.heading: 5. Kingdom Fungi
sections.html: Heterotrophic eukaryotes (except yeast, which is unicellular). The body is a network of thread-like hyphae = mycelium; hyphae may be septate or aseptate/coenocytic. Cell walls contain chitin and polysaccharides. Nutrition is saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic (lichens, mycorrhiza). Reproduction is by spores: asexual (conidia, sporangiospores, zoospores) and sexual (oospores, ascospores, basidiospores). Sexual cycle: plasmogamy → karyogamy → meiosis; in many fungi compatible hyphae fuse before nuclei fuse, giving a dikaryotic (n+n) stage.

sections.heading: 5.1 Phycomycetes
sections.html: Found in aquatic/damp places and on decaying wood; mycelium is aseptate and coenocytic. Asexual spores (zoospores/aplanospores) form in sporangia; sexual spore is the zygospore. Examples: Mucor, Rhizopus (bread mould), Albugo.

sections.heading: 5.2 Ascomycetes (sac fungi)
sections.html: Mostly multicellular (e.g. Penicillium) or unicellular (yeast, Saccharomyces); mycelium branched and septate. Sexual spores = ascospores produced inside sac-like asci arranged in fruiting bodies called ascocarps. Penicillium is a source of antibiotics; Neurospora is used in genetics; some are edible (morels, truffles).

sections.heading: 5.3 Basidiomycetes (club fungi)
sections.html: Mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs; also smuts and rusts. Mycelium is branched and septate. Sexual spores = basidiospores borne externally on club-shaped basidia; fruiting body = basidiocarp. No asexual spores; vegetative reproduction common. Example: Agaricus, Ustilago, Puccinia.

sections.heading: 5.4 Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi)
sections.html: The 'imperfect fungi' — only the asexual / vegetative phase is known. Many are decomposers of litter that help in mineral cycling; some are parasites. Examples: Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma.

sections.heading: 6. Kingdom Plantae
sections.html: Includes all eukaryotic, chlorophyll-containing organisms — algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms. Cells have a cellulose cell wall and a large central vacuole. Mostly autotrophic, but some are insectivorous (Venus flytrap, Nepenthes) or parasitic (Cuscuta). The life cycle shows alternation of generations between a diploid sporophyte and a haploid gametophyte.

sections.heading: 7. Kingdom Animalia
sections.html: Heterotrophic, eukaryotic, multicellular organisms without a cell wall. They have holozoic (ingestive) nutrition, store food as glycogen/fat, and most show tissue/organ/organ-system level organisation, sensory and neuromotor control, and locomotion. They reproduce mostly sexually and show embryological development.

sections.heading: 8. Viruses
sections.html:
Viruses are non-cellular, obligate intracellular entities — inert (crystallisable) outside the host but able to replicate inside a living host. History: D. Ivanowsky discovered them; M.W. Beijerinck coined contagium vivum fluidum (infectious living fluid); W.M. Stanley showed a virus (TMV) could be crystallised.

A virus is essentially a nucleoprotein: genetic material (DNA or RNA, never both) enclosed in a protein coat called the capsid (made of capsomeres); some have an outer envelope. Plant viruses usually have ssRNA, animal viruses ss/dsRNA or dsDNA, and bacteriophages usually dsDNA. Viruses cause diseases such as mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza and AIDS, and plant diseases (mosaic, leaf curling).

sections.heading: 9. Viroids & Prions
sections.html:
Viroids — discovered by T.O. Diener; a free RNA of low molecular weight lacking a protein coat (caused potato spindle tuber disease).

Prions — abnormally folded infectious proteins (no nucleic acid) causing diseases such as BSE (mad cow disease) and CJD.

sections.heading: 10. Lichens
sections.html: Lichens are a symbiotic association between an alga (phycobiont) and a fungus (mycobiont). The alga photosynthesises food; the fungus provides shelter, water and minerals. Lichens grow very slowly and are excellent pollution indicators — they do not grow in polluted (e.g. industrial) areas, so a lichen-free trunk signals high air pollution. (Compare mycorrhiza: a symbiosis between a fungus and the roots of higher plants.)

chapters.title: Plant Kingdom
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 3 covering classification systems and the major plant groups — algae (green, brown, red), bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms — together with their reproduction and the life-cycle patterns (haplontic, diplontic, haplo-diplontic).

sections.heading: 1. Systems of classification
sections.html:
Plant classification has evolved through three kinds of systems:

  • Artificial systems (e.g. Linnaeus) — based on one or a few vegetative or sexual characters; gave equal weight to vegetative and sexual features (which can vary).
  • Natural systems (Bentham & Hooker) — based on natural affinities using all known characters (internal features like anatomy, embryology too).
  • Phylogenetic systems — based on evolutionary relationships.

Numerical taxonomy uses computers and scores hundreds of characters; cytotaxonomy uses cytological information (chromosome number/structure); chemotaxonomy uses chemical constituents.

sections.heading: 2. Algae — general features
sections.html:
Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and largely aquatic organisms. Reproduction is vegetative (fragmentation), asexual (zoospores) and sexual (isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous). They are divided into three classes by pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella.

ChlorophyceaeGreen algaeChlorophyll a, bStarch
PhaeophyceaeBrown algaeChlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthinLaminarin, mannitol
RhodophyceaeRed algaeChlorophyll a, d, phycoerythrin (r-phycoerythrin)Floridean starch

sections.heading: 2.1 Chlorophyceae (green algae)
sections.html: Grass-green due to chlorophyll a and b. Cell wall has an inner cellulose layer; reserve food is starch stored in pyrenoids. Examples: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara.

sections.heading: 2.2 Phaeophyceae (brown algae)
sections.html: Mostly marine; brown colour from fucoxanthin. Stored food is laminarin or mannitol; cell wall has cellulose and algin. Plant body may have a holdfast, stipe and frond. Examples: Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus, Ectocarpus, Dictyota.

sections.heading: 2.3 Rhodophyceae (red algae)
sections.html: Mostly marine (greater depths); red colour from r-phycoerythrin. Stored food is floridean starch. Examples: Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium (sources of agar).

sections.heading: 2.4 Economic importance of algae
sections.html: Algae carry out about half of the total CO₂ fixation (photosynthesis) on Earth and are primary producers. Agar (from Gelidium, Gracilaria) is used in cultures and food; algin (brown algae) and carrageenan (red algae) are commercial hydrocolloids; Porphyra, Laminaria and Sargassum are edible; Chlorella is a protein-rich food supplement.

sections.heading: 3. Bryophytes
sections.html: Bryophytes are the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom' — they live on land but need water for sexual reproduction. The plant body is a gametophyte (more conspicuous), lacking true roots/stem/leaves (has rhizoids). The male sex organ is the antheridium (produces flagellated antherozoids); the female is the archegonium (flask-shaped, produces an egg). The zygote develops into a sporophyte that is attached to and partly dependent on the gametophyte and produces haploid spores by meiosis. Bryophytes help in soil formation and as Sphagnum (peat moss) provide fuel and packing material.

sections.heading: 3.1 Liverworts & Mosses
sections.html: Liverworts (e.g. Marchantia) have a flat, dorsiventral thallus; asexual reproduction by gemmae in gemma cups. Mosses (e.g. Funaria, Sphagnum, Polytrichum) have a protonema stage followed by a leafy gametophore; the moss sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) is more elaborate than that of liverworts.

sections.heading: 4. Pteridophytes
sections.html: Pteridophytes are the first terrestrial plants with vascular tissue (xylem and phloem). The dominant phase is the sporophyte (with true root, stem and leaves). Sporophylls bear sporangia that produce spores by meiosis; spores germinate into small, free-living prothallus (gametophyte), which needs cool, damp, shady places and water for fertilisation. Most are homosporous (one kind of spore); a few (e.g. Selaginella, Salvinia) are heterosporous — producing microspores and megaspores — a precursor to the seed habit. Examples: Selaginella, Equisetum, Pteris, Dryopteris, Lycopodium.

sections.heading: 5. Gymnosperms
sections.html: Gymnosperms bear naked seeds (ovules not enclosed in an ovary; seeds not covered by fruit). They are heterosporous, producing microspores (pollen) and megaspores. Male and female cones (strobili) bear microsporophylls and megasporophylls. The female gametophyte is retained on the parent, and pollination is direct (no water needed). Examples: Cycas, Pinus, Ginkgo, Ephedra. Pinus shows needle leaves; Cycas has coralloid roots with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria; the giant redwood Sequoia is among the tallest trees.

sections.heading: 6. Angiosperms
sections.html: In angiosperms (flowering plants) the seeds are enclosed in fruits. They range from tiny Wolffia to tall Eucalyptus. The flower bears stamens (male, producing pollen) and the pistil/carpel (female, with ovules in the ovary). They show double fertilisation and triple fusion, forming a diploid zygote and triploid endosperm. Angiosperms are divided into dicotyledons (two cotyledons, reticulate venation, tetra/pentamerous flowers) and monocotyledons (one cotyledon, parallel venation, trimerous flowers).

sections.heading: 7. Plant life cycles & alternation of generations
sections.html:
Plants alternate between a haploid gametophyte (n, gamete-producing) and a diploid sporophyte (2n, spore-producing) — the alternation of generations. Three patterns:

  • Haplontic — dominant gametophyte; sporophyte is just the zygote (e.g. many algae, Spirogyra).
  • Diplontic — dominant sporophyte; gametophyte highly reduced (e.g. seed plants — gymnosperms, angiosperms).
  • Haplo-diplontic — both phases multicellular; bryophytes have a dominant gametophyte, while pteridophytes have a dominant sporophyte.

chapters.title: Animal Kingdom
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 4 (Animal Kingdom): the basis of animal classification followed by the diagnostic features and examples of every major phylum from Porifera to Chordata, including the vertebrate classes.

sections.heading: 1. Basis of classification
sections.html:
Despite their diversity, animals are grouped using a few fundamental features:

  • Levels of organisation — cellular (Porifera), tissue (Coelenterata, Ctenophora), organ, and organ-system (Platyhelminthes onward).
  • Symmetry — asymmetrical, radial (Coelenterata, Ctenophora, adult echinoderms) or bilateral (most others).
  • Germ layers — diploblastic (ectoderm + endoderm, with mesoglea: Coelenterata) or triploblastic (ecto-, meso-, endoderm).
  • Coelom — body cavity lined by mesoderm: coelomate (Annelida → Chordata), pseudocoelomate (Aschelminthes) or acoelomate (Platyhelminthes).
  • Segmentation — metameric segmentation (Annelida onward).
  • Notochord — present in chordates (a mesoderm-derived rod); animals without it are non-chordates.

sections.heading: 2. Porifera (sponges)
sections.html: Pore-bearing, mostly marine, asymmetrical animals at the cellular level of organisation. Water enters through minute pores (ostia) into the central cavity (spongocoel) and exits via the osculum; flow is driven by collar cells (choanocytes). They have a water-transport (canal) system and a skeleton of spicules/spongin; reproduction is asexual (budding) and sexual; hermaphrodite, with internal fertilisation and indirect development. Examples: Sycon, Spongilla (freshwater), Euspongia (bath sponge).

sections.heading: 3. Coelenterata (Cnidaria)
sections.html: Aquatic, mostly marine, radially symmetrical, diploblastic, tissue-level animals. They bear stinging cells (cnidoblasts/nematocysts) on tentacles used for anchorage, defence and capturing prey. They have a central gastrovascular cavity with a single opening. Two body forms: sessile polyp (e.g. Hydra, sea anemone) and free-swimming medusa (jellyfish); forms with both show metagenesis (alternation of generations). Corals (e.g. Meandrina) secrete CaCO₃ skeletons. Examples: Hydra, Adamsia (sea anemone), Aurelia (jellyfish), Physalia.

sections.heading: 4. Ctenophora (sea walnuts/comb jellies)
sections.html: Exclusively marine, diploblastic, radially symmetrical, tissue-level animals with eight external rows of ciliated comb plates for locomotion. They show bioluminescence. Fertilisation is external with indirect development. Examples: Pleurobrachia, Ctenoplana.

sections.heading: 5. Platyhelminthes (flatworms)
sections.html: Dorso-ventrally flattened, bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, acoelomate, organ-system level animals; mostly endoparasites. Parasitic forms have hooks and suckers; osmoregulation/excretion by flame cells. Examples: Taenia (tapeworm), Fasciola (liver fluke, internal fertilisation), Planaria (high regeneration), Schistosoma.

sections.heading: 6. Aschelminthes (roundworms / Nematoda)
sections.html: Cylindrical, bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, pseudocoelomate, organ-system level worms; free-living or parasitic. Sexes are separate (dioecious) and females are longer than males; often sexually dimorphic. Examples: Ascaris (roundworm), Wuchereria (filaria), Ancylostoma (hookworm).

sections.heading: 7. Annelida
sections.html: Aquatic or terrestrial, bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, organ-system level, and the first true coelomates. They show metameric segmentation and a closed circulatory system; locomotion by setae or parapodia. Examples: Nereis (dioecious, parapodia), Pheretima (earthworm), Hirudinaria (leech).

sections.heading: 8. Arthropoda
sections.html: The largest phylum; triploblastic, coelomate, organ-system level animals with a chitinous exoskeleton and jointed appendages. Body is divided into head, thorax and abdomen (head + thorax may fuse into a cephalothorax, e.g. in crustaceans). They have compound eyes, an open circulatory system, and respire by gills, book gills/lungs or tracheae; excretion via Malpighian tubules. Examples: Apis (honey bee), Bombyx (silkworm), Anopheles/Culex/Aedes (mosquito vectors), Locusta, Limulus (king crab, a living fossil), scorpion, prawn.

sections.heading: 9. Mollusca
sections.html: Second largest phylum; bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, coelomate, unsegmented soft body usually covered by a calcareous shell. Body has a head, muscular foot and visceral hump covered by a mantle; the mantle cavity has feather-like gills and a rasping radula. Respiratory pigment is haemocyanin (copper-based). Cephalopods (e.g. Octopus, Loligo) have eyes resembling vertebrate eyes. Examples: Pila (apple snail), Pinctada (pearl oyster), Sepia, Chiton.

sections.heading: 10. Echinodermata
sections.html: Exclusively marine; triploblastic, coelomate. Adults show radial symmetry (larvae are bilateral), with an endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles (spiny skin) and a unique water vascular system with tube feet for locomotion, capture and transport. Sexes separate; development indirect. Examples: Asterias (starfish), Echinus (sea urchin), Cucumaria (sea cucumber), Antedon.

sections.heading: 11. Hemichordata
sections.html: Marine, worm-like, bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, coelomate animals with a body of proboscis, collar and trunk. They have a rudimentary structure (stomochord) in the collar — formerly considered a notochord — so they are a link between non-chordates and chordates. Example: Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus.

sections.heading: 12. Chordata — fundamental features & protochordates
sections.html:
Chordates share four fundamental characters: a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits, and a post-anal tail (with a closed circulatory system). Chordata has three subphyla:

  • Urochordata (Tunicata) — notochord only in the larval tail (e.g. Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum).
  • Cephalochordata — notochord extends head to tail and persists (e.g. Branchiostoma/Amphioxus, the lancelet).
  • Vertebrata — notochord replaced by a vertebral column; have a ventral heart, kidneys and paired appendages.

(All vertebrates are chordates, but not all chordates are vertebrates.)

sections.heading: 13. Cyclostomata (jawless fishes)
sections.html: Jawless (Agnatha) vertebrates with a circular sucking mouth, no scales or paired fins, and a cartilaginous skeleton. Many are ectoparasites on fishes. They are marine but migrate to fresh water to spawn. Examples: Petromyzon (lamprey), Myxine (hagfish).

sections.heading: 14. Pisces (fishes)
sections.html:
Aquatic, gill-breathing, cold-blooded vertebrates with fins; the study of fishes is ichthyology. Two classes:

  • Chondrichthyes — cartilaginous fishes; marine; mouth ventral; gill slits without an operculum; placoid scales; males bear claspers on pelvic fins; internal fertilisation; mostly oviparous. Examples: Scoliodon (dogfish), Pristis (sawfish), Trygon (sting ray), Torpedo.
  • Osteichthyes — bony fishes (marine and freshwater); mouth terminal; gills covered by an operculum; cycloid/ctenoid scales; air bladder regulates buoyancy; mostly oviparous, external fertilisation. Examples: Labeo (rohu), Hippocampus (sea horse), Catla, Exocoetus (flying fish), Clarias.

sections.heading: 15. Amphibia
sections.html: Cold-blooded tetrapods that live both on land and in water; skin is moist and without scales; respire by gills, lungs and skin. Heart is three-chambered; mostly oviparous with external fertilisation and indirect development. Examples: Rana (frog), Bufo (toad), Hyla (tree frog), Salamandra, Ichthyophis (limbless caecilian).

sections.heading: 16. Reptilia
sections.html: Creeping, cold-blooded tetrapods with a body covered by dry, scaly skin (epidermal scales); respire by lungs; heart usually three-chambered (four-chambered in crocodiles). They are largely terrestrial, lay shelled eggs on land (internal fertilisation, oviparous). Some snakes are poisonous (cobra, krait, viper). Examples: Chelone (turtle), Testudo (tortoise), Chameleon, Calotes (garden lizard), Naja (cobra), Crocodilus.

sections.heading: 17. Aves (birds)
sections.html: Warm-blooded (homoiothermous) vertebrates adapted for flight: body covered with feathers, forelimbs modified into wings, a beak without teeth, and pneumatic (hollow) bones. The heart is four-chambered; lungs have air sacs; they are oviparous. Examples: Corvus (crow), Columba (pigeon), Psittacula (parrot), Struthio (ostrich), Pavo (peacock), penguin (Aptenodytes).

sections.heading: 18. Mammalia
sections.html: Warm-blooded vertebrates with mammary glands (milk), hair/body fur, external ears (pinnae), a muscular diaphragm and a four-chambered heart; most are viviparous. Reproductive types: oviparous (egg-laying) — Ornithorhynchus (platypus), Echidna; marsupials — Macropus (kangaroo); placental — most others. Bats and whales are mammals (whales bear young and feed milk; bats are the only truly flying mammals). Examples: Homo (man), Panthera, Balaenoptera (blue whale), Pteropus (flying fox).

chapters.title: Morphology of Flowering Plants
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 5: the external form of flowering plants — root, stem and leaf and their modifications, inflorescence, the parts of a flower (symmetry, aestivation, placentation), fruit and seed, the floral formula/diagram, and the semi-technical description of three important families.

sections.heading: 1. The root
sections.html:
The root is the underground, non-green, positively geotropic part. Tap root (from radicle) is typical of dicots; fibrous roots are typical of monocots; adventitious roots arise from parts other than the radicle (e.g. grass, banyan). Regions of the root: root cap, region of meristematic activity, region of elongation, and region of maturation (bearing root hairs).

Modifications: storage — fusiform (radish), conical (carrot), napiform (turnip), tuberous (sweet potato); prop roots (banyan), stilt roots (maize, sugarcane), pneumatophores (respiratory roots of Rhizophora), and nodulated roots (legumes).

sections.heading: 2. The stem
sections.html: The stem develops from the plumule, bears nodes and internodes, buds, and is generally positively phototropic. Modifications: underground food storage — rhizome (ginger), tuber (potato, with 'eyes'), corm (Colocasia), bulb (onion); stem tendrils (cucumber, grapevine) for climbing; thorns (Citrus, Bougainvillea) for protection; phylloclades (Opuntia) and offsets/runners/stolons for vegetative spread.

sections.heading: 3. The leaf
sections.html: The leaf is a lateral, flattened outgrowth of the stem borne at a node; it has a leaf base, petiole and lamina. Venation: reticulate (dicots) vs parallel (monocots). Types: simple vs compound (pinnately compound — neem; palmately compound — silk cotton). Phyllotaxy (arrangement on stem): alternate (china rose, mustard, sunflower), opposite (Calotropis), whorled (Alstonia). Modifications: tendrils (pea), spines (cactus), phyllode (Australian acacia), pitcher (Nepenthes), storage (onion fleshy leaves).

sections.heading: 4. Inflorescence
sections.html: The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis. Racemose — main axis continues to grow, flowers borne laterally in acropetal order (younger at top), e.g. mustard, radish. Cymose — main axis terminates in a flower, so growth is limited, flowers in basipetal order, e.g. Solanum, jasmine.

sections.heading: 5. The flower — parts, symmetry & aestivation
sections.html:
A flower is a modified shoot with four whorls on the thalamus: calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens — male) and gynoecium (carpels — female). A flower with all four whorls is complete; with both androecium and gynoecium it is bisexual.

Symmetry: actinomorphic (radial — mustard, chilli), zygomorphic (bilateral — pea, gulmohur) or asymmetric (canna). Position of floral parts w.r.t. ovary: hypogynous (superior ovary), perigynous, epigynous (inferior ovary). Aestivation (arrangement of sepals/petals in bud): valvate (Calotropis), twisted (china rose), imbricate (Cassia, gulmohur) and vexillary (pea — five petals: standard, two wings, two keel).

sections.heading: 6. Placentation
sections.html: The arrangement of ovules on the placenta within the ovary: marginal (pea), axile (china rose, tomato, lemon), parietal (mustard, Argemone), free central (Dianthus, Primrose) and basal (sunflower, marigold).

sections.heading: 7. Fruit & seed
sections.html: The fruit is the mature ovary; a fruit formed from the ovary alone is true, while a false fruit develops from the thalamus too (e.g. apple). Parthenocarpic fruits form without fertilisation (banana). A fruit has pericarp (epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp) and seed(s); in a drupe (mango, coconut) the endocarp is stony. A seed has seed coat(s) and an embryo (radicle, plumule, cotyledon[s]) — dicot seeds have two cotyledons, monocot seeds (maize) one cotyledon with endosperm.

sections.heading: 8. Floral formula & diagram
sections.html: A floral formula represents a flower with symbols: ⊕ actinomorphic, % zygomorphic; ♂ male, ♀ female, ⚥ bisexual; K = calyx, C = corolla, P = perianth, A = androecium, G = gynoecium; superscript number = parts; brackets = fusion; line above G = inferior ovary, line below = superior ovary. The floral diagram shows the number, arrangement and aestivation of parts as seen in a cross-section, with the mother axis marked.

sections.heading: 9. Important families
sections.html:
• Fabaceae (Papilionoideae) — e.g. pea, gram, bean. Zygomorphic, bisexual flowers; vexillary aestivation; stamens (9)+1 (diadelphous); superior ovary, marginal placentation; fruit a legume. Source of pulses, oil, dyes (indigo).
  • Solanaceae — e.g. potato, tomato, brinjal, tobacco. Actinomorphic, bisexual; calyx and corolla 5, valvate; stamens 5 epipetalous; bicarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary with axile placentation, placenta swollen; fruit a berry/capsule.
  • Liliaceae — e.g. lily, onion, garlic, Aloe. Monocot; flowers trimerous, actinomorphic; perianth of 3+3 tepals; 6 stamens; tricarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary, axile placentation; fruit a capsule/berry.

chapters.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 6: the internal structure of flowering plants — meristematic and permanent tissues, the three tissue systems, the anatomy of dicot vs monocot roots, stems and leaves, and secondary growth.

sections.heading: 1. Meristematic tissues
sections.html: Meristems are groups of actively dividing cells. Apical meristems occur at root and shoot tips (primary growth, increase in length). Intercalary meristems lie at the base of internodes/leaves (also primary). Lateral meristems (vascular cambium and cork cambium) are cylindrical and add to girth (secondary growth). Cells cut off by meristems mature into permanent tissues (differentiation).

sections.heading: 2. Simple permanent tissues
sections.html:
• Parenchyma — living, thin-walled, isodiametric cells; perform photosynthesis, storage and secretion (chlorenchyma if chloroplast-bearing; aerenchyma stores air in hydrophytes).
  • Collenchyma — living cells with cellulose/pectin thickening at the corners; give mechanical support and flexibility to growing organs (e.g. petioles, dicot stems).
  • Sclerenchyma — dead cells with thick lignified walls; provide mechanical strength. Two types: long, pointed fibres and variously shaped sclereids (stone cells of guava/pear).

sections.heading: 3. Complex permanent tissues (xylem & phloem)
sections.html: Xylem conducts water and minerals upward and gives support; elements: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres (all dead) and living xylem parenchyma. Phloem conducts food (sugars); elements: sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres. In gymnosperms vessels are absent in xylem and companion cells/sieve tubes are absent in phloem (replaced by albuminous cells and sieve cells). Protoxylem matures first; metaxylem later. In roots xylem and phloem are on different radii (exarch, radial); in stems they form joint bundles.

sections.heading: 4. The three tissue systems
sections.html:
• Epidermal tissue system — the outer protective layer: epidermis (one layer), cuticle, stomata (guarded by bean-shaped guard cells in dicots, dumb-bell shaped in grasses) and epidermal appendages (root hairs, trichomes).
  • Ground tissue system — all cells except epidermis and vascular bundles: cortex, endodermis, pericycle, pith and medullary rays (mostly parenchyma).
  • Vascular tissue system — the vascular bundles (xylem + phloem). Radial in roots; conjoint in stems. Conjoint bundles are open (cambium present → secondary growth, dicot stem) or closed (no cambium, monocot stem).

sections.heading: 5. Dicot vs monocot root
sections.html: Both have epidermis (epiblema with root hairs), cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle and radial vascular bundles with exarch protoxylem. Dicot root: usually 2–4 (di- to tetrarch) xylem groups, with a small pith and a cambium that appears later (secondary growth). Monocot root: polyarch (many xylem bundles), large well-developed pith, no secondary growth.

sections.heading: 6. Dicot vs monocot stem
sections.html: Dicot stem: vascular bundles arranged in a ring, conjoint, collateral, open (with cambium), endarch protoxylem; well-differentiated cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle and pith. Monocot stem: vascular bundles scattered in ground tissue, conjoint, collateral and closed (no cambium, no secondary growth); bundles surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; ground tissue not differentiated; often a water-containing cavity in the protoxylem.

sections.heading: 7. Leaf anatomy (dorsiventral vs isobilateral)
sections.html: Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf: mesophyll differentiated into upper palisade and lower spongy parenchyma; stomata mainly on the lower surface. Isobilateral (monocot) leaf: mesophyll not differentiated; stomata on both surfaces; some epidermal cells enlarge into bulliform cells that roll the leaf to reduce water loss. Vascular bundles lie in the veins (larger in midrib).

sections.heading: 8. Secondary growth
sections.html: Secondary growth increases girth, mainly in dicot stems and roots. The vascular cambium forms a complete ring (interfascicular + intrafascicular cambium) and cuts off secondary xylem (wood) inward and secondary phloem outward. Spring/early wood (wide vessels) and autumn/late wood (narrow vessels) make annual rings used to estimate age. The cork cambium (phellogen) produces cork (phellem) outside and secondary cortex (phelloderm) inside — together the periderm; lenticels allow gaseous exchange. Old wood is dark, non-conducting heartwood; outer light sapwood conducts.

chapters.title: Structural Organisation in Animals
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 7: the four animal tissue types (epithelial, connective, muscular, neural) and the morphology and anatomy of three representative animals — earthworm, cockroach and frog.

sections.heading: 1. Epithelial tissue
sections.html: A single layer of closely packed cells resting on a basement membrane, with a free surface; it covers/lines body surfaces and cavities. Simple epithelium (one layer): squamous (flat — alveoli, blood-vessel walls; for diffusion), cuboidal (ducts, kidney tubules; secretion/absorption), columnar (stomach, intestine), and ciliated (bronchioles, oviduct; moves particles/mucus). Compound epithelium has many layers (skin, buccal cavity) for protection. Glandular epithelium forms exocrine (duct) and endocrine (ductless) glands. Cells are held by cell junctions: tight junctions (prevent leakage), adhering junctions (cement cells) and gap junctions (allow communication).

sections.heading: 2. Connective tissue
sections.html: Most abundant and widely distributed; cells secrete fibres (collagen/elastin) in a matrix. Loose connective tissue: areolar (beneath skin, with fibroblasts, mast cells, macrophages) and adipose (stores fat). Dense connective tissue: dense regular (tendons — muscle to bone; ligaments — bone to bone) and dense irregular (skin). Specialised connective tissue: cartilage (matrix of chondroitin, cells in lacunae — chondrocytes), bone (hard calcium matrix, osteocytes in lacunae), and blood (fluid matrix = plasma; a vascular connective tissue).

sections.heading: 3. Muscular tissue
sections.html: Made of elongated muscle fibres (myocytes). Skeletal (striated/voluntary) muscle — attached to bones, striped, multinucleate, fatigues. Smooth (visceral/non-striated, involuntary) muscle — walls of internal organs (stomach, intestine, blood vessels), spindle-shaped, uninucleate. Cardiac muscle — only in the heart, striated but involuntary, branched, with intercalated discs; does not fatigue.

sections.heading: 4. Neural tissue
sections.html: Neurons are excitable cells (the unit of the nervous system) that receive and transmit impulses; supported by neuroglial cells. A neuron has a cell body, dendrites and an axon; when stimulated, a wave of disturbance (nerve impulse) is conducted along it.

sections.heading: 5. Earthworm (Pheretima)
sections.html: A reddish-brown, segmented (metameric) annelid; a 'farmer's friend'. The dorsal side has a darker mid-dorsal line (blood vessel); the ventral side bears genital openings. The first segment is the peristomium with an overhanging prostomium; segments 14–16 form a glandular band, the clitellum (dividing the body into pre-clitellar, clitellar and post-clitellar regions). Locomotion uses S-shaped setae. They are hermaphrodite (testes in segments 10–11, ovaries in 12–13) but show cross-fertilisation. The alimentary canal runs straight (mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → gizzard → stomach → intestine → anus); typhlosole increases absorption. Excretion by nephridia; closed circulatory system; respiration through moist skin.

sections.heading: 6. Cockroach (Periplaneta)
sections.html: A brown-black arthropod; body divided into head, thorax and abdomen covered by a chitinous exoskeleton of sclerites (tergites dorsal, sternites ventral). Head bears compound eyes and antennae; three thoracic segments each bear a pair of legs (two pairs of wings on meso- and metathorax). Abdomen has 10 segments; males bear anal styles (females lack them). Digestion: mouthparts (mandibles) → crop (storage) → gizzard/proventriculus (grinding, with chitinous teeth); hepatic caeca secrete enzymes. Open circulatory system with a 13-chambered heart; respiration via tracheae opening through spiracles; excretion by Malpighian tubules. Blood is colourless (haemolymph). Sexes separate, sexually dimorphic.

sections.heading: 7. Frog (Rana tigrina)
sections.html: A cold-blooded (poikilothermic) amphibian showing camouflage and aestivation/hibernation. Skin is moist and naked for cutaneous respiration; respires also by buccal cavity and lungs. Body is head + trunk (no neck/tail in adult). Three-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle) with single circulation portal systems (hepatic and renal portal). Digestive, respiratory, circulatory, excretory (mesonephric kidney), nervous and reproductive systems are well developed. Sexes are separate; males have vocal sacs and copulatory pads; fertilisation is external and development indirect (tadpole → metamorphosis).

chapters.title: Cell: The Unit of Life
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 8: the cell theory, the distinction between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and the structure and function of every cell organelle — membrane, wall, endomembrane system, mitochondria, plastids, ribosomes, cytoskeleton and nucleus.

sections.heading: 1. Cell theory & overview
sections.html: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. Robert Hooke first saw dead cells (cork); Leeuwenhoek saw live cells. The cell theory — all living organisms are made of cells and cell products — was given by Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals), and extended by Rudolf Virchow with Omnis cellula-e cellula (all cells arise from pre-existing cells). Cells vary in size (the smallest are Mycoplasma, ~0.3 µm; the largest cell is an ostrich egg) and shape (disc-like RBCs, branched neurons, long fibres).

sections.heading: 2. Prokaryotic cells
sections.html: Found in bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma and PPLO. They lack a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles. The genetic material is a single circular DNA (nucleoid, no nuclear membrane), often with extra plasmids. The cell envelope has a glycocalyx, a cell wall and plasma membrane; the Gram stain divides them into Gram-positive and Gram-negative. Mesosomes (membrane infoldings) aid respiration, secretion and DNA replication; some have chromatophores for photosynthesis. Ribosomes are 70S; motile forms have flagella; pili and fimbriae are surface structures. Inclusion bodies store reserve material.

sections.heading: 3. Cell (plasma) membrane
sections.html: Described by the fluid mosaic model of Singer & Nicolson (1972): a bilayer of phospholipids with proteins (integral and peripheral) floating in it; the quasi-fluid lipid allows lateral movement (membrane fluidity). It is selectively permeable. Transport: passive (diffusion, osmosis — no energy, down the gradient) and active (against the gradient, using ATP, e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump). Polar molecules need carrier proteins.

sections.heading: 4. Cell wall
sections.html: A non-living rigid outer layer of plant/fungal cells giving shape and protection. The plant cell wall has a middle lamella (calcium pectate, cements cells), a primary wall (cellulose) and, in mature cells, a secondary wall. Adjacent cells are connected by plasmodesmata. Algae have cellulose, galactans and minerals; fungi have chitin.

sections.heading: 5. Endomembrane system (ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles)
sections.html:
• Endoplasmic reticulum — network of tubules. Rough ER (RER) bears ribosomes and makes/secretes proteins; Smooth ER (SER) lacks ribosomes and makes lipids/steroids.
  • Golgi apparatus — stacked cisternae; packages, modifies and dispatches materials (glycosylation, glycolipid/glycoprotein formation); the cis (forming) face faces the ER, the trans (maturing) face the membrane.
  • Lysosomes — Golgi-derived vesicles rich in hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes active at acidic pH; the cell's 'suicide bags'.
  • Vacuoles — membrane (tonoplast)-bound; the large plant vacuole stores sap and maintains turgor; contractile vacuoles in protists do osmoregulation.

sections.heading: 6. Mitochondria
sections.html: The 'powerhouse of the cell' — site of aerobic respiration producing ATP. Double-membraned: the inner membrane is folded into cristae bearing F₁ (oxysome) particles; the inner space is the matrix (contains enzymes of the Krebs cycle, circular DNA and 70S ribosomes — so mitochondria are semi-autonomous and self-replicating).

sections.heading: 7. Plastids
sections.html: Found in plant cells. Chloroplasts (green, with chlorophyll) carry out photosynthesis — double membrane, with stacked thylakoids (grana) embedded in the stroma (which holds enzymes, circular DNA and 70S ribosomes). Chromoplasts contain carotenoid pigments (yellow/orange/red). Leucoplasts are colourless storage plastids: amyloplasts (starch), elaioplasts (oils/fats), aleuroplasts (proteins).

sections.heading: 8. Ribosomes
sections.html: Non-membranous granules of rRNA and protein — the site of protein synthesis. Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S (60S + 40S subunits); prokaryotic and those of mitochondria/chloroplasts are 70S (50S + 30S). They occur free in the cytoplasm or attached to the RER; several on one mRNA form a polysome.

sections.heading: 9. Cytoskeleton, cilia, flagella & centrosome
sections.html: The cytoskeleton (microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments) gives shape, support and enables movement. Cilia and flagella are membrane-covered projections with a 9 + 2 microtubule arrangement (axoneme) arising from a basal body; cilia move fluids, flagella move the cell. The centrosome has two centrioles with a 9 + 0 (9 triplets, no centre) cartwheel arrangement; centrioles form the basal bodies and the spindle fibres during division.

sections.heading: 10. Nucleus
sections.html: The control centre, bounded by a double nuclear envelope with nuclear pores and continuous with the ER. It contains nucleoplasm, one or more nucleoli (sites of rRNA synthesis/ribosome assembly) and chromatin (DNA + histone proteins) that condenses into chromosomes during division. A chromosome has a centromere with kinetochores; by centromere position chromosomes are metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric or telocentric; a satellite chromosome bears a secondary constriction.

sections.heading: 11. Microbodies
sections.html: Microbodies are tiny membrane-bound vesicles containing enzymes, present in plant and animal cells — e.g. peroxisomes (photorespiration, H₂O₂ breakdown) and glyoxysomes (fat-rich germinating seeds).

chapters.title: Biomolecules
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 9: the chemical constituents of living cells — amino acids, proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids — and a detailed look at enzymes and the metabolic state of the cell.

sections.heading: 1. Analysis & types of biomolecules
sections.html: Chemical analysis: an acid-soluble pool of micromolecules (MW < 1000 Da — amino acids, sugars, nucleotides) and an acid-insoluble fraction of macromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides; lipids stay in this fraction though small). Primary metabolites (amino acids, sugars) have direct roles in physiology; secondary metabolites (alkaloids, rubber, pigments, drugs) have ecological/commercial roles. By mass in a cell, water is most abundant; among macromolecules proteins are the most abundant, and overall carbohydrates are abundant in the biosphere (cellulose).

sections.heading: 2. Amino acids
sections.html: Amino acids are substituted methanes with an amino (–NH₂) group, a carboxyl (–COOH) group, an H and a variable R group on the same α-carbon. About 20 occur in proteins; based on R they are acidic (glutamic acid), basic (lysine), neutral, aromatic, etc. They are zwitterionic (ionisable, so charge changes with pH). Nine are essential (must be taken in diet).

sections.heading: 3. Proteins
sections.html: Proteins are polypeptides — amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Levels of structure: primary (sequence), secondary (helix/sheet), tertiary (3-D folding), and quaternary (assembly of subunits, e.g. haemoglobin's four chains). Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world; RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere. Proteins act as enzymes, transporters (GLUT-4), antibodies, hormones, receptors and structural elements.

sections.heading: 4. Carbohydrates
sections.html: Polyhydroxy aldehydes/ketones. Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose) cannot be hydrolysed; disaccharides (sucrose, lactose, maltose) and polysaccharides form on linking by glycosidic bonds. Storage polysaccharides: starch (plants — forms a helix that gives a blue colour with iodine) and glycogen (animals); structural: cellulose (plant cell wall, no helices), chitin and inulin (fructose polymer).

sections.heading: 5. Lipids
sections.html: Generally water-insoluble. Fatty acids (e.g. palmitic, arachidonic) may be saturated or unsaturated. Glycerides (fats and oils) are esters of glycerol with fatty acids; oils have a low melting point (liquid in winter, e.g. gingelly oil). Phospholipids (lecithin) have a phosphate group and are key membrane lipids.

sections.heading: 6. Nucleic acids
sections.html: Polymers of nucleotides; each nucleotide = a nitrogenous base + a pentose sugar (ribose/deoxyribose) + a phosphate. Bases: purines (adenine, guanine) and pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine in DNA / uracil in RNA). Nucleotides join through 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds. DNA and RNA are the genetic/expression molecules (detailed in Ch 6, Class XII).

sections.heading: 7. Enzymes
sections.html: Enzymes are biological catalysts (almost all proteins; some RNAs are ribozymes). They have an active site into which the substrate fits (the substrate forms an enzyme–substrate complex); they greatly lower the activation energy. Properties: highly specific, reusable, and sensitive to temperature and pH (each has an optimum; high temperature denatures them). Activity is also affected by substrate concentration and inhibitors (competitive inhibition, e.g. malonate on succinic dehydrogenase). Classified into six classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases. Many need cofactors: prosthetic groups, coenzymes (often vitamin-derived, e.g. NAD/FAD) and metal ion activators; the protein part alone is the apoenzyme, and with cofactor the active holoenzyme.

sections.heading: 8. Metabolism & the living state
sections.html: Thousands of metabolic reactions occur in the cell, organised into pathways (anabolic — build-up, use energy; catabolic — break-down, release energy). Metabolites are constantly interconverted (a dynamic state) and pooled (the metabolic pool). The living state is a non-equilibrium steady state maintained by the continuous flow of metabolism — work is possible only because the system is not at equilibrium.

chapters.title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 10: the phases of the cell cycle, mitosis (equational division) and meiosis (reductional division), and the significance of each.

sections.heading: 1. The cell cycle
sections.html: The cell cycle is the sequence of events between two divisions. In a typical human cell (~24 h) it has two broad phases: interphase (the long preparatory phase) and the M phase (division). Interphase = G₁ (cell grows, metabolically active), S (DNA replication — DNA doubles but chromosome number stays the same; centriole also duplicates) and G₂ (growth, preparation for mitosis). Non-dividing cells exit into a quiescent G₀ stage. In animal cells division uses a centriolar spindle; plants lack centrioles.

sections.heading: 2. Mitosis (M phase)
sections.html:
Mitosis is equational — the daughter cells get the same chromosome number as the parent. It occurs in somatic cells. Karyokinesis (nuclear division) has four stages:

  • Prophase — chromosomes condense (each with two chromatids joined at the centromere); spindle begins to form; nuclear envelope and nucleolus disappear.
  • Metaphase — chromosomes align at the equatorial (metaphase) plate; spindle fibres attach to kinetochores. Best stage to study chromosome morphology.
  • Anaphase — centromeres split and sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
  • Telophase — chromosomes decondense; nuclear envelope and nucleolus reappear.

Cytokinesis (cytoplasmic division) follows: a cleavage furrow in animal cells, a cell plate forming from centre outward in plant cells. Mitosis enables growth, repair and cell replacement, keeping the genome constant.

sections.heading: 3. Meiosis
sections.html:
Meiosis is reductional — two successive divisions (meiosis I and II) with DNA replicated only once, giving four haploid cells from one diploid cell; it occurs in germ cells and ensures gamete/spore formation. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes; Meiosis II is mitosis-like (separates sister chromatids).

Prophase I is long, with five sub-stages: Leptotene (chromosomes condense) → Zygotene (synapsis: homologous chromosomes pair forming bivalents/synaptonemal complex) → Pachytene (crossing over — recombination between non-sister chromatids, catalysed by recombination nodules) → Diplotene (homologues separate but stay joined at chiasmata) → Diakinesis (terminalisation of chiasmata, nuclear envelope breaks down). In Metaphase I bivalents align; in Anaphase I homologous chromosomes (not chromatids) separate.

sections.heading: 4. Significance of meiosis
sections.html: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so fertilisation restores the diploid number across generations (genome stability of a species). Crossing over and the random assortment of homologous chromosomes generate genetic variation — the raw material for evolution.

chapters.title: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 11: how green plants make food — the early experiments, photosynthetic pigments, the light reaction and photophosphorylation, the Calvin (C3) cycle, the C4 pathway, photorespiration and the factors that limit photosynthesis.

sections.heading: 1. Site & early experiments
sections.html: Photosynthesis occurs in the chloroplast (mainly in mesophyll cells); the membrane (thylakoid) system carries out the light reaction and the stroma the dark (biosynthetic) reactions. Landmark experiments: Joseph Priestley (plants purify air — O₂); Ingenhousz (light and green parts needed); Julius von Sachs (glucose/starch produced in chloroplasts); T.W. Engelmann (action spectrum using Cladophora + aerobic bacteria — red and blue light most effective); Cornelius van Niel (the O₂ released comes from water, not CO₂).

sections.heading: 2. Photosynthetic pigments
sections.html: Pigments in the thylakoids: chlorophyll a (the chief/primary pigment, bright/blue-green), chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids (accessory/antenna pigments that also protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation). The absorption spectrum shows maxima in the blue and red regions; the action spectrum of photosynthesis closely follows the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a, confirming it as the main pigment.

sections.heading: 3. Light reaction (photochemical phase)
sections.html: In the thylakoids, light is absorbed by two photosystems — PS I (reaction centre P700) and PS II (P680). In non-cyclic flow electrons pass PS II → cytochrome → PS I → NADP⁺ (the Z-scheme), forming NADPH. PS II splits water (photolysis) on the inner thylakoid side, releasing O₂, protons and electrons; this is the source of evolved oxygen. So the light reaction yields ATP, NADPH and O₂.

sections.heading: 4. Photophosphorylation & chemiosmosis
sections.html: ATP synthesis in light is photophosphorylation. Non-cyclic (both PS I and PS II) produces ATP + NADPH + O₂; cyclic (only PS I, electrons cycle back) produces only ATP (occurs in stroma lamellae / when only PS I is active or NADP⁺ is unavailable). ATP forms by chemiosmosis: a proton gradient builds across the thylakoid membrane (protons accumulate in the lumen) and flows out through ATP synthase (CF₀–CF₁).

sections.heading: 5. Calvin cycle (C3 pathway)
sections.html: The dark reaction (biosynthetic phase) fixes CO₂ in the stroma using ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle has three stages: Carboxylation — CO₂ + the 5-C acceptor RuBP → two 3-C 3-PGA molecules, catalysed by RuBisCO (the first stable product is 3-PGA, a 3-carbon acid → 'C3'); Reduction — PGA → G3P (triose phosphate), using ATP and NADPH; Regeneration — RuBP is regenerated (uses ATP). To make one glucose, the cycle turns 6 times, using 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

sections.heading: 6. C4 pathway
sections.html: C4 plants (e.g. maize, sugarcane, sorghum) show special Kranz anatomy — large, chloroplast-rich bundle-sheath cells around the vascular bundles. The primary CO₂ acceptor is PEP (3-C) and the enzyme is PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells; the first product is the 4-C acid OAA (→ malate). Malate releases CO₂ in bundle-sheath cells, where the Calvin cycle then runs — concentrating CO₂ around RuBisCO. C4 plants are more efficient, lack photorespiration, and tolerate higher temperatures.

sections.heading: 7. Photorespiration
sections.html: RuBisCO has affinity for both CO₂ and O₂. When O₂ is high, it acts as an oxygenase: RuBP + O₂ → one PGA + one 2-C phosphoglycolate (the C2 cycle). Photorespiration does not produce ATP, NADPH or sugar — it is a wasteful process in C3 plants. C4 plants avoid it by keeping CO₂ high around RuBisCO.

sections.heading: 8. Factors affecting photosynthesis
sections.html: Rate depends on light, CO₂, temperature (external) and chlorophyll/leaf factors (internal). Blackman's Law of Limiting Factors: when several factors affect a process, the rate is set by the factor in shortest supply (the limiting factor). For most C3 plants under field light, CO₂ is the major limiting factor; light saturation occurs at ~10% of full sunlight.

chapters.title: Respiration in Plants
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 12: how cells release energy from food — glycolysis, fermentation, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation, and the energetics (ATP yield, RQ, amphibolic pathway).

sections.heading: 1. Cellular respiration — overview
sections.html: Cells break C–C bonds of respiratory substrates in a controlled, stepwise oxidation to release energy stored as ATP. The common substrate is glucose; fats, proteins and organic acids can also be respired. Respiration may be aerobic (needs O₂, complete oxidation) or anaerobic (no O₂, incomplete). The Respiratory Quotient (RQ) = CO₂ released / O₂ consumed — 1 for carbohydrates, <1 for fats (~0.7), >1 for organic acids.

sections.heading: 2. Glycolysis (EMP pathway)
sections.html: The Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas (EMP) pathway occurs in the cytoplasm and is common to aerobic and anaerobic respiration. One glucose (6-C) is converted to two pyruvate (3-C). Net gain: 2 ATP (substrate-level) and 2 NADH. It is the first step of glucose breakdown in all living organisms.

sections.heading: 3. Fermentation (anaerobic respiration)
sections.html: Without O₂, pyruvate is incompletely oxidised to regenerate NAD⁺. Alcoholic fermentation (yeast) → ethanol + CO₂ (enzymes pyruvate decarboxylase, alcohol dehydrogenase). Lactic acid fermentation (some bacteria, exercising muscle) → lactic acid. Fermentation yields less than 7% of glucose's energy (only the 2 ATP of glycolysis) and is hazardous (alcohol/acid build-up).

sections.heading: 4. Krebs cycle (TCA / citric acid cycle)
sections.html: In aerobic respiration, pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix and is oxidatively decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA (by pyruvate dehydrogenase, giving 1 NADH + 1 CO₂). Acetyl-CoA (2-C) combines with OAA (4-C) to form citrate (6-C), starting the Krebs cycle. Per pyruvate the cycle yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP (GTP) and releases 2 CO₂; OAA is regenerated.

sections.heading: 5. Electron transport chain & oxidative phosphorylation
sections.html: NADH and FADH₂ are oxidised in the inner mitochondrial membrane through complexes I–IV (with ubiquinone and cytochrome c); electrons finally reduce O₂ to water (the terminal acceptor, via complex IV / cytochrome oxidase). The energy pumps protons to build a gradient that drives ATP synthase (F₀–F₁, complex V) — this is oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis). Each NADH ≈ 3 ATP and each FADH₂ ≈ 2 ATP.

sections.heading: 6. Energetics & amphibolic pathway
sections.html: Complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose yields a net of about 36–38 ATP. Respiration is an amphibolic pathway — it both breaks down (catabolic) and provides intermediates for the synthesis (anabolic) of fats, amino acids, etc. Fats are broken to acetyl-CoA, proteins to keto acids before entering respiration. (Aerobic respiration is far more efficient than fermentation.)

chapters.title: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 14: respiratory organs, the mechanism of breathing, exchange and transport of O₂ and CO₂, regulation of respiration, and disorders of the respiratory system.

sections.heading: 1. Overview & steps of respiration
sections.html: Breathing (pulmonary ventilation) is the exchange of atmospheric O₂ with alveolar CO₂. Respiration in animals involves: (i) breathing — inspiration and expiration; (ii) diffusion of O₂ and CO₂ across the alveolar membrane; (iii) transport of gases by blood; (iv) tissue exchange; (v) cellular respiration (Ch 12). Lower invertebrates exchange gases by simple diffusion; earthworms use the moist cuticle; insects use tracheae; aquatic forms use gills; terrestrial vertebrates use lungs. Amphibians also respire through moist skin (cutaneous respiration).

sections.heading: 2. Human respiratory system
sections.html: Air enters through external nostrils → nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx (cartilaginous sound box; epiglottis covers glottis during swallowing) → trachea (incomplete cartilaginous rings) → right/left primary bronchi (at 5th thoracic vertebra) → secondary/tertiary bronchi → bronchioles → thin vascular alveoli (site of gas exchange). The conducting part (nostrils to terminal bronchioles) warms, humidifies and filters air; the exchange part (alveoli and ducts) is where diffusion occurs. Lungs lie in the airtight thoracic cavity (vertebral column, sternum, ribs, diaphragm), covered by double-layered pleura with pleural fluid reducing friction.

sections.heading: 3. Mechanism of breathing
sections.html: Inspiration: contraction of the diaphragm (increases thoracic volume antero-posteriorly) and external intercostal muscles (lift ribs/sternum, dorso-ventral axis) → thoracic and pulmonary volume increase → intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric → air flows in. Expiration: relaxation of diaphragm and intercostals → thoracic volume decreases → intrapulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric → air expelled. Forced breathing uses abdominal muscles. Average rate: 12–16 breaths/min. A spirometer measures pulmonary volumes.

sections.heading: 4. Respiratory volumes & capacities
sections.html:
• Tidal Volume (TV) — air inspired/expired per normal breath (~500 mL).
  • IRV — extra inspired forcibly (~2500–3000 mL).
  • ERV — extra expired forcibly (~1000–1100 mL).
  • RV — air left after forced expiration (~1100–1200 mL).
  • IC = TV + IRV; EC = TV + ERV.
  • FRC = ERV + RV (after normal expiration).
  • VC = ERV + TV + IRV (max breath in/out).
  • TLC = VC + RV (total lung capacity).

sections.heading: 5. Exchange of gases
