sections.html: Exchange at alveoli and tissues occurs by simple diffusion down partial-pressure gradients. Partial pressure (pO₂, pCO₂) drives movement: O₂ from alveoli (pO₂ ~104 mm Hg) to deoxygenated blood (~40) to tissues; CO₂ in the opposite direction. CO₂ is 20–25× more soluble than O₂, so more diffuses per unit gradient. The diffusion membrane = alveolar squamous epithelium + basement membrane + capillary endothelium (<1 mm thick). Rate depends on gradient, solubility and membrane thickness.

sections.heading: 6. Transport of oxygen
sections.html: ~97% of O₂ is carried by RBCs bound to haemoglobin (oxyhaemoglobin, reversible; max 4 O₂ per Hb); ~3% dissolved in plasma. Binding depends on pO₂, pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature. The oxygen dissociation curve (sigmoid) shows % saturation vs pO₂. At alveoli (high pO₂, low pCO₂, low H⁺, lower T) Hb loads O₂; at tissues (low pO₂, high pCO₂, high H⁺, higher T) O₂ is released. Every 100 mL oxygenated blood delivers ~5 mL O₂ to tissues.

sections.heading: 7. Transport of carbon dioxide
sections.html: CO₂ transport: ~70% as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻, via carbonic anhydrase: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻); ~20–25% as carbamino-haemoglobin; ~7% dissolved. At tissues (high pCO₂) CO₂ enters blood → bicarbonate; at alveoli (low pCO₂) reaction reverses → CO₂ released. The chloride shift balances ionic charge. ~100 mL deoxygenated blood delivers ~4 mL CO₂ to alveoli.

sections.heading: 8. Regulation of respiration
sections.html: The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla sets the basic breathing pattern. The pneumotaxic centre in the pons moderates it (shortens inspiration). A chemosensitive area near the rhythm centre responds to ↑CO₂ and H⁺. Peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery also detect CO₂/H⁺ changes. O₂ plays a minor role in normal regulation. Neural control allows breathing to match tissue demands (e.g. exercise, altitude).

sections.heading: 9. Disorders of the respiratory system
sections.html:
• Asthma — bronchi/bronchiole inflammation → wheezing, difficulty breathing.
  • Emphysema — alveolar wall damage (often smoking) → reduced respiratory surface.
  • Occupational respiratory disorders — dust (grinding, stone-breaking) → inflammation, fibrosis; workers need protective masks.

chapters.title: Body Fluids and Circulation
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 15: blood and lymph, circulatory pathways, the human heart and cardiac cycle, double circulation, regulation of cardiac activity, and disorders of the circulatory system.

sections.heading: 1. Overview — body fluids & circulation
sections.html: Higher animals transport nutrients, O₂ and wastes via specialised fluids. Blood is the main body fluid; lymph (tissue fluid) assists transport. Circulation may be open (arthropods, molluscs — blood into sinuses) or closed (annelids, chordates — blood in vessels). All vertebrates have a muscular chambered heart; pattern varies from 2-chambered (fish) to 4-chambered (birds, mammals).

sections.heading: 2. Plasma
sections.html: Plasma is straw-coloured, viscous (~55% of blood); ~90–92% water, 6–8% proteins (fibrinogen — clotting; globulins — defence; albumin — osmotic balance). Contains minerals (Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, HCO₃⁻, Cl⁻), glucose, amino acids, lipids and inactive clotting factors. Serum = plasma without clotting factors.

sections.heading: 3. Formed elements
sections.html: ~45% of blood. RBCs (erythrocytes) — most abundant (~5–5.5 million/mm³), biconcave, enucleate in mammals, contain haemoglobin (12–16 g/100 mL), lifespan ~120 days, destroyed in spleen. WBCs (leucocytes) — ~6000–8000/mm³; granulocytes (neutrophils 60–65%, eosinophils 2–3%, basophils 0.5–1%) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes 20–25%, monocytes 6–8%). Platelets (thrombocytes) — 1.5–3.5 lakh/mm³, fragments from megakaryocytes, essential for clotting.

sections.heading: 4. Blood groups (ABO & Rh)
sections.html: ABO — based on A/B antigens on RBCs and anti-A/anti-B antibodies in plasma: A (anti-B), B (anti-A), AB (no antibodies, universal recipient), O (anti-A,B; universal donor). Rh — Rh antigen on RBCs (~80% Rh⁺). Rh⁻ exposed to Rh⁺ blood forms anti-Rh antibodies. Erythroblastosis foetalis — Rh⁻ mother, Rh⁺ foetus in subsequent pregnancies; prevented by anti-Rh after first delivery.

sections.heading: 5. Coagulation of blood
sections.html: Injury triggers clotting to prevent blood loss. A clot (coagulum) is a fibrin mesh trapping damaged cells. Thrombokinase activates prothrombin → thrombin, which converts fibrinogen → fibrin (cascade process). Platelets and tissue factors initiate the cascade. Ca²⁺ is essential.

sections.heading: 6. Lymph (tissue fluid)
sections.html: As blood passes through capillaries, water and small solutes leave into intercellular spaces → tissue/interstitial fluid (same mineral distribution as plasma, minus most proteins). The lymphatic system collects this as lymph (colourless, with lymphocytes) and returns it to major veins. Lymph carries nutrients, hormones; lacteals in intestinal villi absorb fats.

sections.heading: 7. Circulatory pathways
sections.html: Fish — 2-chambered heart, single circulation (heart → gills → body → heart). Amphibians/reptiles (except crocodile) — 3-chambered, incomplete double circulation (mixed blood in single ventricle). Crocodiles, birds, mammals — 4-chambered, complete double circulation (no mixing). Closed system allows precise flow regulation.

sections.heading: 8. Human heart & conduction system
sections.html: Mesodermal, fist-sized, in thoracic cavity between lungs, tilted left, in pericardium. Four chambers: right/left atria (upper), right/left ventricles (lower, thicker walls). Tricuspid (RA→RV), bicuspid/mitral (LA→LV), semilunar valves (RV→pulmonary artery, LV→aorta) ensure one-way flow. Nodal tissue: SAN (pacemaker, 70–75 impulses/min) → AVN → AV bundle (Bundle of His) → Purkinje fibres. Heart is myogenic (autoexcitable).

sections.heading: 9. Cardiac cycle
sections.html: Sequential systole and diastole (~0.8 s, ~72 cycles/min). Joint diastole → SAN fires → atrial systole (~30% extra filling) → ventricular systole (AV valves close — 'lub'; semilunar open → blood to pulmonary artery/aorta) → ventricular diastole (semilunar close — 'dub'). Stroke volume ~70 mL; cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate ≈ 5 L/min.

sections.heading: 10. Electrocardiogram (ECG)
sections.html: Graphical record of heart's electrical activity. P wave — atrial depolarisation; QRS complex — ventricular depolarisation/contraction onset; T wave — ventricular repolarisation. Heart rate = QRS complexes per minute. Deviations indicate abnormalities.

sections.heading: 11. Double circulation & blood vessels
sections.html: Pulmonary circulation: RV → pulmonary artery → lungs (O₂ pickup) → pulmonary veins → LA. Systemic circulation: LV → aorta → tissues → vena cava → RA. Vessels have three layers: tunica intima, media, externa. Hepatic portal system — intestine → liver → systemic circulation. Coronary circulation supplies cardiac muscle.

sections.heading: 12. Regulation of cardiac activity
sections.html: Intrinsic (nodal tissue) plus neural/hormonal modulation. Medullary cardiac centre via ANS: sympathetic ↑rate and contractility; parasympathetic (vagus) ↓rate and conduction. Adrenal medullary hormones (adrenaline/noradrenaline) increase cardiac output.

sections.heading: 13. Disorders of circulatory system
sections.html:
• Hypertension — BP persistently >140/90 mm Hg.
  • CAD/atherosclerosis — arterial plaque narrows coronary vessels.
  • Angina — chest pain from insufficient O₂ to heart muscle.
  • Heart failure — heart cannot pump effectively (≠ cardiac arrest or heart attack).

chapters.title: Excretory Products and Their Elimination
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 16: nitrogenous waste excretion, the human excretory system, urine formation, counter-current mechanism, regulation of kidney function, and disorders.

sections.heading: 1. Overview — excretion & nitrogenous wastes
sections.html: Metabolism produces wastes (ammonia, urea, uric acid, CO₂, ions) that must be eliminated. Major nitrogenous wastes: ammonia (most toxic, needs much water — ammonotelic: bony fishes, aquatic amphibians/insects), urea (ureotelic: mammals, terrestrial amphibians, marine fishes), uric acid (uricotelic: reptiles, birds, insects, land snails — minimal water loss).

sections.heading: 2. Excretory structures in animals
sections.html: Protonephridia/flame cells — Platyhelminthes, rotifers, Amphioxus (osmoregulation). Nephridia — annelids (earthworm). Malpighian tubules — insects. Antennal/green glands — crustaceans. Kidneys — vertebrate excretory organs.

sections.heading: 3. Human excretory system
sections.html: Pair of kidneys (bean-shaped, 10–12 × 5–7 × 2–3 cm, ~120–170 g), ureters, urinary bladder, urethra. Kidney: hilum (ureter, vessels, nerves), renal pelvis with calyces, outer cortex, inner medulla (pyramids), Columns of Bertini. ~1 million nephrons per kidney.

sections.heading: 4. Nephron structure
sections.html: Functional unit: glomerulus (afferent → efferent arteriole capillary tuft) + Bowman's capsule = Malpighian/renal corpuscle. Tubule: PCT → Henle's loop (descending + ascending) → DCT → collecting duct → renal pelvis. Cortical nephrons (short loop); juxtamedullary nephrons (long loop into medulla). Peritubular capillaries and vasa recta (U-shaped, parallel to Henle's loop) surround tubules.

sections.heading: 5. Urine formation
sections.html: Three processes: glomerular filtration (ultrafiltration through endothelium, basement membrane, podocyte slits; proteins retained; GFR ~125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day), reabsorption (~99% of filtrate returned) and tubular secretion (H⁺, K⁺, NH₃). JGA (juxtaglomerular apparatus) regulates GFR via renin when flow/pressure falls.

sections.heading: 6. Function of nephron segments
sections.html: PCT — brush border; reabsorbs ~70–80% water, electrolytes, all glucose/amino acids; secretes H⁺, NH₃. Henle's loop — descending limb permeable to water; ascending impermeable to water, transports electrolytes (builds medullary osmolarity). DCT — conditional Na⁺/water reabsorption; H⁺/K⁺/NH₃ secretion. Collecting duct — water reabsorption (concentrated urine), urea recycling, pH/ionic balance.

sections.heading: 7. Counter-current mechanism
sections.html: Opposing flow in Henle's loop limbs and vasa recta creates a medullary osmolarity gradient (300 → ~1200 mOsmol L⁻¹) via NaCl and urea transport. Enables collecting duct to produce urine ~4× concentrated over initial filtrate — vital water conservation.

sections.heading: 8. Regulation of kidney function
sections.html: ADH/vasopressin (hypothalamus, osmoreceptors) — ↑water reabsorption in distal tubule/collecting duct. Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (JGA) — renin → angiotensin II (vasoconstriction, ↑GFR) → aldosterone (↑Na⁺/water reabsorption). ANF (atria, ↑blood volume) — vasodilation, opposes RAAS. Together maintain blood volume, pressure and osmolarity.

sections.heading: 9. Micturition
sections.html: Urine stored in bladder until ~200–300 mL stretches walls → stretch receptors → CNS → motor signals → bladder smooth muscle contracts, urethral sphincter relaxes → micturition (micturition reflex; voluntary override in adults). Normal output ~1–1.5 L/day; urine slightly acidic (pH ~6), ~25–30 g urea/day.

sections.heading: 10. Role of other organs in excretion
sections.html: Lungs — CO₂ (~200 mL/min) and water vapour. Liver — bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin), cholesterol, steroids, drugs. Skin — sweat (NaCl, urea, lactic acid); sebaceous glands (sebum: sterols, waxes). Small nitrogenous wastes in saliva.

sections.heading: 11. Disorders of excretory system
sections.html:
• Uraemia — urea accumulation; treated by haemodialysis (artificial kidney) or kidney transplant.
  • Renal calculi — kidney stones (oxalates, etc.).
  • Glomerulonephritis — glomerular inflammation.
  • Glycosuria/ketonuria — diagnostic of diabetes mellitus.

chapters.title: Locomotion and Movement
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 17: types of movement, muscle structure and contraction, the skeletal system, joints, and disorders of the muscular and skeletal systems.

sections.heading: 1. Movement & locomotion
sections.html: Living organisms show diverse movements. Human cells exhibit amoeboid (macrophages, leucocytes), ciliary (trachea, oviduct) and muscular movements. Locomotion is voluntary movement changing body position (walking, running, swimming). All locomotion involves movement but not vice versa. Locomotion aids food, shelter, mate and escape.

sections.heading: 2. Types of muscles
sections.html: Muscle (~40–50% body weight) — mesodermal, excitable, contractile, extensible, elastic. Skeletal (striated, voluntary) — attached to skeleton, striped, multinucleate. Smooth (visceral, non-striated, involuntary) — hollow organs (GI tract, vessels), spindle-shaped, uninucleate. Cardiac — heart only, striated, branched, involuntary, intercalated discs.

sections.heading: 3. Skeletal muscle structure
sections.html: Muscle → fascicles (bundles) → muscle fibres (syncytium: sarcolemma, multinucleate sarcoplasm, rich sarcoplasmic reticulum storing Ca²⁺). Each fibre has parallel myofibrils with alternating dark A bands (myosin) and light I bands (actin). Z line bisects each I band. Sarcomere = region between two Z lines (functional contractile unit). H zone = central thick-filament only region.

sections.heading: 4. Contractile proteins
sections.html: Actin (thin) — F-actin (polymer of G-actin) + tropomyosin + troponin (troponin masks myosin-binding sites at rest). Myosin (thick) — polymer of meromyosins (HMM head with ATPase + actin-binding sites; LMM tail). Cross-bridges form between myosin heads and actin during contraction.

sections.heading: 5. Mechanism of muscle contraction
sections.html: Sliding filament theory: CNS → motor neuron → neuromuscular junction (ACh release) → action potential in sarcolemma → Ca²⁺ from SR → Ca²⁺ binds troponin → actin sites exposed → myosin cross-bridges (ATP hydrolysis) pull actin → sarcomere shortens (I band and H zone shrink; A band unchanged). Ca²⁺ pumped back → relaxation. Repeated stimulation → lactic acid → fatigue. Red fibres (myoglobin-rich, aerobic); white fibres (less myoglobin, anaerobic).

sections.heading: 6. Skeletal system overview
sections.html: 206 bones and cartilages — specialised connective tissue (bone: hard Ca²⁺ matrix; cartilage: pliable chondroitin matrix). Two divisions: axial (80 bones) and appendicular. Supports movement, protects organs, provides muscle attachment.

sections.heading: 7. Axial skeleton
sections.html: Skull (22 bones: 8 cranial + 14 facial), hyoid, 3 ear ossicles/ear (malleus, incus, stapes), vertebral column (26 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacral fused, 1 coccygeal fused; atlas articulates with occipital condyles — dicondylic skull), sternum, 12 pairs of ribs (7 true, 3 false/vertebrochondral, 2 floating) forming rib cage.

sections.heading: 8. Appendicular skeleton & girdles
sections.html: Each limb = 30 bones. Forelimb: humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges. Hindlimb: femur (longest bone), tibia, fibula, patella, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges. Pectoral girdle — scapula + clavicle (glenoid cavity with humerus). Pelvic girdle — two coxal bones (ilium, ischium, pubis fused; acetabulum with femur); pubic symphysis ventrally.

sections.heading: 9. Joints
sections.html: Points of contact between bones/cartilage; muscles act through joints as levers. Fibrous — immovable (skull sutures). Cartilaginous — limited movement (intervertebral discs). Synovial — fluid-filled cavity, freely movable: ball-and-socket (shoulder), hinge (knee, elbow), pivot (atlas-axis), gliding (carpals), saddle (thumb carpometacarpal).

sections.heading: 10. Disorders of muscular & skeletal system
sections.html:
• Myasthenia gravis — autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder.
  • Muscular dystrophy — progressive skeletal muscle degeneration.
  • Tetany — rapid spasms from low Ca²⁺.
  • Arthritis — joint inflammation.
  • Osteoporosis — age-related bone mass loss (↓estrogen).
  • Gout — uric acid crystals in joints.

chapters.title: Neural Control and Co-ordination
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 18: neural coordination — the human nervous system (CNS and PNS), neuron structure, resting and action potentials, synaptic transmission, and the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.

sections.heading: 1. Neural system & coordination
sections.html: Organs must be coordinated so their activities complement one another (e.g. during exercise: muscles, lungs, heart and kidneys work together). The neural system gives rapid point-to-point connections; the endocrine system gives slower chemical integration via hormones. Neurons are highly specialised cells that detect, receive and transmit stimuli. Organisation is simple in lower invertebrates (e.g. Hydra — a nerve net); better in insects (brain + ganglia); most developed in vertebrates.

sections.heading: 2. Human neural system (CNS & PNS)
sections.html: CNS — brain + spinal cord (information processing and control). PNS — all nerves linked to the CNS. Nerve fibres: afferent (sensory → CNS) and efferent (CNS → effectors). PNS divisions: somatic (to skeletal muscles) and autonomic (to involuntary organs/smooth muscle) — further split into sympathetic and parasympathetic. The visceral nervous system is the PNS component linking viscera and CNS.

sections.heading: 3. Neuron — structure & types
sections.html: A neuron has a cell body (with Nissl's granules), dendrites (conduct impulses toward the cell body) and an axon (conducts away; ends in synaptic knobs with neurotransmitter vesicles). Types by processes: multipolar (one axon, ≥2 dendrites — cerebral cortex), bipolar (one each — retina), unipolar (one process — embryonic). Axons may be myelinated or non-myelinated.

sections.heading: 4. Myelinated & non-myelinated fibres
sections.html: Myelinated fibres are wrapped by Schwann cells forming a myelin sheath; gaps between sheaths are nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction). Found in spinal and cranial nerves. Non-myelinated fibres have Schwann cells without a myelin sheath — common in autonomic and somatic systems. Myelination greatly speeds impulse conduction.

sections.heading: 5. Resting & action potentials
sections.html: At rest the axonal membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) maintains ionic gradients — outer surface positive, inner negative → resting potential (~−70 mV). A stimulus opens Na⁺ channels → rapid Na⁺ influx → depolarisation → action potential (nerve impulse). Local currents depolarise adjacent regions; K⁺ efflux restores resting potential (repolarisation). Includes absolute/relative refractory periods.

sections.heading: 6. Synaptic transmission
sections.html: Impulses pass between neurons at synapses (pre- and post-synaptic membranes, optionally separated by a synaptic cleft). Electrical synapses — membranes very close, direct current flow; always faster but rare. Chemical synapses — neurotransmitters released from synaptic vesicles bind post-synaptic receptors, opening ion channels → excitatory or inhibitory post-synaptic potentials.

sections.heading: 7. Brain — protection & major divisions
sections.html: The brain is protected by the skull and cranial meninges: outer dura mater, thin arachnoid, inner pia mater (on brain tissue). Three major parts: forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain. The brain stem (midbrain + pons + medulla) connects brain to spinal cord. Controls voluntary movement, balance, vital organs, thermoregulation, hunger/thirst, circadian rhythms, endocrine glands, behaviour, vision, hearing, speech, memory and emotions.

sections.heading: 8. Forebrain
sections.html: Comprises cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus. Cerebrum — two hemispheres linked by corpus callosum; outer cerebral cortex (grey matter — motor, sensory and association areas) over inner white matter (myelinated tracts). Thalamus — major sensory/motor relay. Hypothalamus — body temperature, eating/drinking, neurosecretory cells releasing hypothalamic hormones. Limbic system (with hypothalamus) — emotion, motivation, sexual behaviour.

sections.heading: 9. Midbrain & hindbrain
sections.html: Midbrain — between thalamus/hypothalamus and pons; cerebral aqueduct passes through it; dorsal corpora quadrigemina (four lobes) integrate visual, tactile and auditory inputs. Hindbrain — pons (fibre tracts linking brain regions), cerebellum (convoluted surface; coordinates balance/movement using vestibular and auditory input) and medulla oblongata (connected to spinal cord; centres for respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions).

sections.heading: 10. Reflex action
sections.html: A reflex is a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus via a reflex arc (receptor → sensory neuron → integration centre in CNS → motor neuron → effector). Spinal reflexes (e.g. knee-jerk, withdrawal reflex) bypass conscious brain processing for speed. The simplest reflex arc involves one sensory and one motor neuron (monosynaptic).

sections.heading: 11. Eye & vision
sections.html: The eyeball wall layers (inside → out): retina, choroid, sclera. Retina has rods (dim light) and cones (colour/bright light); contains bipolar neurons. Iris controls pupil diameter; lens focuses light (held by suspensory ligament/Zonule of Zinn). Rhodopsin (visual purple) in rods needs vitamin A. Cornea and lens refract light; vitreous chamber filled with vitreous humour.

sections.heading: 12. Ear & hearing
sections.html: Ear: outer (pinna, ear canal, tympanic membrane), middle (ossicles — malleus, incus, stapes linking tympanum to oval window) and inner (bony labyrinth with perilymph; membranous labyrinth with endolymph). Cochlea — organ of Corti and sound reception. Vestibular apparatus — semicircular canals (angular acceleration) and utricle/saccule with otolith organs/maculae (gravity/linear acceleration). Scala vestibuli and scala tympani filled with perilymph.

chapters.title: Chemical Coordination and Integration
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 19: chemical coordination through hormones — the human endocrine glands (hypothalamus–pituitary axis, thyroid, adrenals, pancreas, gonads and others), hormones of heart/kidney/GI tract, and mechanisms of hormone action.

sections.heading: 1. Endocrine glands & hormones
sections.html: Endocrine glands are ductless; their secretions (hormones) are non-nutrient intercellular messengers produced in trace amounts. Contrast exocrine glands (with ducts). The neural system gives fast, short-lived coordination; hormones give slower, sustained regulation. Major endocrine organs: hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, adrenal, pancreas and gonads; heart, kidney and GI tract also secrete hormones.

sections.heading: 2. Hypothalamus & pituitary
sections.html: Hypothalamus neurosecretory nuclei release releasing and inhibiting hormones (via hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system) to control the anterior pituitary; directly regulates posterior pituitary. Pituitary in sella turcica: adenohypophysis (pars distalis + pars intermedia) and neurohypophysis (pars nervosa). Anterior hormones: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH, MSH. Posterior stores/releases oxytocin and vasopressin (ADH) made in hypothalamus. GH excess → gigantism/acromegaly; deficiency → dwarfism. ADH deficiency → diabetes insipidus.

sections.heading: 3. Pineal & thyroid glands
sections.html: Pineal (dorsal forebrain) secretes melatonin — regulates circadian rhythms (sleep–wake, body temperature, menstrual cycle). Thyroid — two lobes + isthmus; follicles secrete T₃ and T₄ (need dietary iodine). Regulate BMR, growth/CNS development, erythropoiesis and carbohydrate/protein/fat metabolism. Also secretes thyrocalcitonin (TCT) lowering blood Ca²⁺. Iodine deficiency → goitre/cretinism; excess → hyperthyroidism (Graves'/exophthalmic goitre).

sections.heading: 4. Parathyroid & thymus
sections.html: Parathyroid (four glands on thyroid posterior) secretes PTH — raises blood Ca²⁺ via bone resorption, renal reabsorption and intestinal absorption (hypercalcemic; works with TCT). Thymus (behind sternum) secretes thymosins — T-lymphocyte differentiation (cell-mediated immunity) and antibody production (humoral immunity). Thymus degenerates with age → weaker immunity in the elderly.

sections.heading: 5. Adrenal gland
sections.html: One gland above each kidney. Adrenal medulla — adrenaline/epinephrine and noradrenaline/norepinephrine (catecholamines; emergency/fight-or-flight hormones: alertness, pupil dilation, sweating, ↑ heart rate/respiration, glycogenolysis). Adrenal cortex zones: zona glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids — aldosterone, Na⁺ reabsorption), zona fasciculata/reticularis (glucocorticoids — cortisol: gluconeogenesis, anti-inflammatory) plus small androgens. Cortex underproduction → Addison's disease.

sections.heading: 6. Pancreas (endocrine)
sections.html: Composite gland — exocrine (digestive enzymes) + endocrine Islets of Langerhans (α and β cells). Glucagon (α) — hyperglycemic: glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in liver. Insulin (β) — hypoglycemic: enhances glucose uptake/utilisation and glycogenesis in hepatocytes and adipocytes. Together maintain glucose homeostasis. Prolonged hyperglycemia → diabetes mellitus (treated with insulin).

sections.heading: 7. Testis & ovary
sections.html: Testis (scrotum) — Leydig cells secrete androgens/testosterone: male accessory sex organ development, secondary sexual characters, spermatogenesis, libido, anabolic effects. Ovary — growing follicles secrete estrogens (secondary sex characters, follicle growth, mammary development); post-ovulation corpus luteum secretes progesterone (pregnancy maintenance, mammary alveoli and milk secretion).

sections.heading: 8. Heart, kidney & GI hormones
sections.html: Heart atria — ANF (atrial natriuretic factor) lowers blood pressure (vasodilation). Kidney juxtaglomerular cells — erythropoietin stimulates RBC formation. GI tract endocrine cells: gastrin (HCl/pepsinogen), secretin (pancreatic H₂O/HCO₃⁻), CCK (pancreatic enzymes + bile), GIP (inhibits gastric secretion/motility).

sections.heading: 9. Mechanism of hormone action
sections.html: Hormones bind specific receptors on target cells. Membrane-bound receptors (peptide/protein hormones, catecholamines) generate second messengers (cAMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺). Intracellular/nuclear receptors (steroids, thyroid hormones) enter the cell and regulate gene expression. Hormone classes: peptides, steroids, iodothyronines and amino-acid derivatives (e.g. epinephrine). One receptor per hormone — high specificity.

chapters.title: Transport in Plants
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 11: how water and minerals move through plant cells, tissues and the whole plant — diffusion, osmosis, water potential, pathways in roots, root pressure, the cohesion–tension theory of xylem sap ascent, transpiration and phloem translocation.

sections.heading: 1. Transport at different levels
sections.html: Plants are less mobile than animals and need a specialised system for uptake, transport and storage of water, nutrients and photosynthates. Transport occurs at three levels: (i) cell to cell — short distances across membranes and through plasmodesmata; (ii) tissue level — movement through vascular tissues; (iii) whole plant — long-distance transport in xylem and phloem. Water and minerals absorbed by roots move upward through the xylem; organic solutes (mainly sucrose) are translocated through the phloem from source to sink.

sections.heading: 2. Diffusion, facilitated diffusion & osmosis
sections.html: Diffusion is the passive movement of substances along a concentration gradient — gases and small lipophilic molecules cross membranes directly. Facilitated diffusion uses membrane channel and carrier proteins (no ATP); it is faster than simple diffusion and shows saturation kinetics. Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a semi-permeable membrane. In a hypotonic solution cells swell (may burst in animal cells); in hypertonic solution they shrink (exosmosis — excessive fertiliser can cause water stress this way); in isotonic solution there is no net water movement.

sections.heading: 3. Water potential (Ψ)
sections.html: Water potential (Ψ) is the potential energy of water per unit volume relative to pure water. Pure water at standard temperature has Ψ = 0 (the reference). Solute lowers Ψ (solute potential Ψs, always negative); pressure raises Ψ (pressure potential Ψp). Ψ = Ψp + Ψs. Water moves from a region of higher (less negative) Ψ to lower (more negative) Ψ. In a flaccid plant cell Ψp ≈ 0; in a turgid cell Ψp is positive.

sections.heading: 4. Imbibition
sections.html: Imbibition is the swelling of solid colloids when they absorb water — a type of diffusion where water is adsorbed with a large increase in volume and development of imbibition pressure. Classic examples: dry seeds and wood absorbing water (prehistoric man used swelling wood to split rocks). Imbibition requires hydrophilic colloids and a water potential gradient.

sections.heading: 5. Active transport & mineral uptake
sections.html: Active transport moves ions/molecules against a concentration gradient using ATP and carrier proteins. Plant roots absorb mineral ions from soil; uptake is selective and can be inhibited by anaerobic conditions (lack of ATP). Membrane proteins for facilitated diffusion and active transport show enzyme-like properties: saturation, specificity and sensitivity to inhibitors.

sections.heading: 6. Apoplastic & symplastic pathways
sections.html: Water in roots can move by two pathways: Apoplastic — through cell walls and intercellular spaces (does not cross living membranes until the Casparian strip of the endodermis blocks further apoplastic movement); Symplastic — through cytoplasm via plasmodesmata, cell to cell. Most water in roots ultimately enters the xylem via the symplast after crossing endodermal cells.

sections.heading: 7. Root pressure & guttation
sections.html: Root pressure is the positive pressure developed in xylem when ions are actively pumped into the stele and water follows osmotically — it can push water a few metres and is seen when transpiration is low. Guttation (water droplets at leaf margins through hydathodes) is caused by root pressure, not transpiration. Root pressure alone cannot account for water rise in tall trees.

sections.heading: 8. Xylem transport & cohesion–tension
sections.html: Water rises in xylem mainly by the transpiration pull (cohesion–tension theory): evaporation from leaves creates tension; the continuous water column is pulled upward. The cohesive and adhesive properties of water maintain the column. Transpiration pull and root pressure act as pulling and pushing forces respectively. In rooted plants xylem transport of water and minerals is essentially unidirectional (upward).

sections.heading: 9. Transpiration
sections.html: Transpiration is loss of water vapour from aerial parts, mainly through stomata (also cuticle and lenticels). Guard cells regulate stomatal aperture. Factors affecting rate: light, temperature, humidity, wind and available soil water. Adaptations to reduce water loss include sunken stomata, thick cuticle and C₄/Kranz anatomy. At higher altitude (lower atmospheric pressure) transpiration rate increases. Plants obtain most carbon from the atmosphere (CO₂), not soil.

sections.heading: 10. Phloem translocation
sections.html: Organic solutes (mainly sucrose) are translocated through sieve tube members from source (photosynthetic leaves, storage organs) to sink (roots, fruits, growing tips). Source and sink can reverse seasonally (e.g. tap root as source in early spring). The pressure-flow (mass-flow) hypothesis explains translocation: loading at source raises Ψ, unloading at sink lowers it, generating bulk flow. P-proteins and companion cells support sieve-tube function.

chapters.title: Mineral Nutrition
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 12: essential mineral elements, criteria of essentiality, macro- and micronutrients, deficiency symptoms, the nitrogen cycle, biological nitrogen fixation and hydroponics.

sections.heading: 1. Essential mineral elements
sections.html: Plants obtain minerals from soil solution. Of ~105 known elements, 17 are essential for plant growth. They are classified by quantitative requirement: macronutrients (C, H, O, N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S — needed in large amounts) and micronutrients (Fe, Mn, Cu, Mo, B, Zn, Cl, Ni — needed in traces). Structural elements of the cell are C, H, O, N; P is required for all phosphorylation reactions.

sections.heading: 2. Criteria of essentiality & critical concentration
sections.html: Arnon and Stout criteria: (i) essential for completing life cycle; (ii) requirement is specific, not replaceable; (iii) directly involved in metabolism. Critical concentration is the concentration of an essential element below which plant growth is retarded — deficiency symptoms appear first in younger or older tissues depending on whether the element is mobile or immobile (e.g. Ca, S, Fe are not remobilised; N, P, K are).

sections.heading: 3. Hydroponics
sections.html: Hydroponics (solution culture) — growing plants in nutrient solution without soil — was demonstrated by Julius von Sachs (1860). A balanced nutrient solution contains all essential elements in proper proportion. Used to identify essential elements and study deficiency; commercially used for vegetables and flowers.

sections.heading: 4. Mineral absorption & soil
sections.html: Soil supplies minerals, anchors roots and holds water. Mineral ions are absorbed mainly by root epidermal cells — active transport (needs ATP); absorption is inhibited in anaerobic conditions. Calcium affects permeability of the plasma membrane. Toxic concentration of minerals causes damage; excess of one element can induce deficiency of another.

sections.heading: 5. Macronutrients — functions & deficiency
sections.html:
• Nitrogen — component of proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll; deficiency → chlorosis, stunted growth.
  • Phosphorus — nucleic acids, ATP, membrane lipids; deficiency → purple/reddish leaves, poor root growth.
  • Potassium — enzyme activation, stomatal opening, ion balance; deficiency → yellowing of leaf margins.
  • Calcium — cell wall (middle lamella), membrane stability; not remobilised.
  • Magnesium — central atom of chlorophyll; activates many enzymes.
  • Sulphur — constituent of amino acids (cysteine, methionine); deficiency causes chlorosis.

sections.heading: 6. Micronutrients — functions & deficiency
sections.html:
• Iron (Fe) — chlorophyll synthesis (not a constituent); deficiency → interveinal chlorosis.
  • Manganese (Mn) — photolysis of water in PS II; deficiency → grey spots of oats.
  • Zinc (Zn) — auxin synthesis; deficiency → rosette habit, little leaves.
  • Copper (Cu) — component of plastocyanin and cytochrome oxidase.
  • Boron (B) — pollen germination, cell wall synthesis.
  • Molybdenum (Mo) — essential for nitrogen fixation and nitrate reduction.
  • Chlorine (Cl) — water splitting in photosynthesis.

sections.heading: 7. Nitrogen cycle
sections.html: Atmospheric N₂ is fixed, assimilated by plants, passed through food chains, returned by decomposition and denitrification. Steps: nitrogen fixation → ammonification → nitrification (NH₃ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻) → uptake → denitrification (NO₃⁻ back to N₂). Industrial and biological fixation replenish usable nitrogen.

sections.heading: 8. Biological nitrogen fixation
sections.html: Rhizobium (and related genera) forms root nodules on legumes (groundnut, soybean). Leg-haemoglobin (pink pigment) protects nitrogenase from O₂. Nitrogenase (Mo, Fe, protein cofactor — not Mg) reduces N₂ to ammonia (first stable product in legumes). Free-living fixers include Azotobacter, Anabaena. Nitrogenase may need low O₂ (anaerobic conditions in nodules).

sections.heading: 9. Special nutritional modes
sections.html: Insectivorous plants (e.g. pitcher plant, Venus flytrap) grow in nitrogen-deficient soil and trap insects for nutrition — an example of nutritional adaptation. Mycorrhiza — symbiotic association of fungi with roots — helps absorb phosphorus and other minerals. Delay in flowering can occur due to deficiency of N, P or K.

chapters.title: Plant Growth and Development
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 13: growth (meristems, phases, growth rates), differentiation, dedifferentiation, development and plasticity, the five plant growth regulators (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene, ABA), and photoperiodism/vernalisation.

sections.heading: 1. Growth — definition & measurement
sections.html: Growth is an irreversible permanent increase in size/mass/number of cells, accompanied by anabolic and catabolic metabolism. At the cellular level growth is principally an increase in protoplasm. It is measured by fresh/dry weight, length, area, volume or cell number. Growth requires water (turgor for cell enlargement), oxygen, nutrients and optimum temperature.

sections.heading: 2. Meristems & indeterminate growth
sections.html: Plant growth is generally indeterminate — meristems retain dividing capacity throughout life (open form of growth). Root and shoot apical meristems give primary growth (elongation); lateral meristems (vascular cambium, cork cambium) give secondary growth (girth). A maize root apex can produce >17,500 cells/hour.

sections.heading: 3. Phases of growth
sections.html: Three phases along a root/shoot axis: meristematic (dividing, thin walls, dense protoplasm) → elongation (vacuolation, cell enlargement) → maturation (wall thickening, differentiation). Slow initial growth = lag phase; rapid exponential increase = log phase; slowing = senescent phase.

sections.heading: 4. Growth rates & curves
sections.html: Arithmetic growth: one daughter cell continues dividing (e.g. root elongating at constant rate; Lt = L₀ + rt). Geometric growth: both progeny divide (exponential; W₁ = W₀ert). Plotted against time → sigmoid (S) curve (lag → log → stationary). Absolute growth rate = total growth per unit time; relative growth rate = growth per unit initial size.

sections.heading: 5. Differentiation, dedifferentiation & redifferentiation
sections.html: Differentiation — cells mature structurally/functionally (e.g. tracheary elements lose protoplasm, develop lignified secondary walls). Dedifferentiation — differentiated cells regain division capacity (e.g. interfascicular cambium from parenchyma). Redifferentiation — dedifferentiated cells mature again. Differentiation in plants is open — same meristem gives different tissues depending on position.

sections.heading: 6. Development & plasticity
sections.html: Development includes all changes from germination to senescence — broadly growth + differentiation. Plasticity allows different pathways in response to environment (e.g. heterophylly in cotton, coriander, larkspur; buttercup leaves differ in air vs water). Intrinsic factors include plant growth regulators; extrinsic include light, temperature, water, nutrition.

sections.heading: 7. Plant growth regulators — overview
sections.html: PGRs (phytohormones) are small molecules: auxins (indole compounds), gibberellins (terpenes), cytokinins (adenine derivatives), ABA (carotenoid derivative), ethylene (gas). Promoters (auxin, GA, cytokinin) stimulate division/enlargement/flowering; inhibitors (ABA, ethylene) regulate dormancy, abscission, stress. Discovery milestones: Darwin (phototropism/coleoptile tip), Went (auxin), Kurosawa (gibberellin), Skoog/Miller (kinetin), Cousins (ethylene).

sections.heading: 8. Auxins
sections.html: Natural: IAA, IBA; synthetic: NAA, 2,4-D. Synthesised at shoot/root apices. Effects: cell elongation, apical dominance (removal of shoot tip → lateral buds grow — used in tea hedges), rooting of cuttings, parthenocarpy (tomato), prevent early fruit/leaf drop, promote abscission of older leaves, xylem differentiation, herbicide (2,4-D kills dicot weeds, not mature monocots). Highest auxin concentration in growing tips.

sections.heading: 9. Gibberellins
sections.html: Over 100 GAs (GA₁, GA₃…); GA₃ most studied; all acidic. Effects: stem/axis elongation (grape stalks, sugarcane yield ↑ ~20 t/acre), bolting in rosette plants (beet, cabbage), overcome seed dormancy, delay senescence, speed up malting in brewing, hasten maturity of conifers, elongate apple fruits. ABA is often antagonistic to GA.

sections.heading: 10. Cytokinins
sections.html: Discovered as kinetin from herring sperm DNA; natural forms include zeatin (corn kernels, coconut milk). Promote cytokinesis, new leaves, chloroplast development, lateral shoot growth, adventitious buds; overcome apical dominance; delay leaf senescence via nutrient mobilisation. Used in tissue culture with auxin.

sections.heading: 11. Ethylene
sections.html: Gaseous PGR from ripening/senescing tissues. Promotes fruit ripening (respiratory climacteric), senescence and abscission, breaks seed/bud dormancy, horizontal growth of seedlings, root hair formation (increases absorption surface), flowering in mango/pineapple. Commercial source: ethephon. Ripe fruit releases ethylene → hastens ripening of nearby unripe fruit.

sections.heading: 12. Abscisic acid (ABA)
sections.html: Growth inhibitor; discovered as inhibitor-B/abscission II/dormin. Stress hormone — stimulates stomatal closure, induces seed dormancy (withstands desiccation), promotes abscission, inhibits germination. Seed dormancy is largely due to ABA. Antagonistic to gibberellins in many processes.

sections.heading: 13. Photoperiodism & vernalisation
sections.html: Photoperiodism (Garner & Allard) — effect of day/night length on flowering. Short-day plants flower when day length < critical period (uninterrupted long night); long-day plants when day > critical; day-neutral (tomato, maize) flower in any photoperiod. Perceived in leaves via phytochrome (chromoprotein; PR ⇌ PFR). Vernalisation — low-temperature treatment promoting flowering. A defoliated plant cannot respond to photoperiod.

sections.heading: 14. Plant movements & seed dormancy
sections.html: Phototropism — growth toward light (Darwin coleoptile experiments). Thigmotropism — coiling of pea tendrils around support. Seed dormancy — viable seeds fail to germinate despite favourable conditions (hard/impermeable seed coat, ABA); overcome by scarification or GA treatment. Germination requires favourable temperature, water, oxygen.

chapters.title: Digestion and Absorption
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XI Chapter 16: the human alimentary canal, digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, the role of liver, pancreas and intestinal juice, absorption in the small intestine and assimilation of nutrients.

sections.heading: 1. Digestion — overview & alimentary canal
sections.html: Digestion converts complex food into simple absorbable forms. The alimentary canal is a continuous muscular tube: mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus (posterior opening). Wall layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, serosa. The canal and associated glands (salivary, liver, pancreas) form the digestive system.

sections.heading: 2. Buccal cavity & teeth
sections.html: The mouth has teeth, tongue and salivary glands. Teeth cut and masticate food; enamel is the hardest substance in the vertebrate body. Normal adult human dental formula: I 2/2, C 1/1, PM 2/2, M 3/3 (2123/2123). Saliva contains salivary amylase (ptyalin) — begins starch digestion (~30% hydrolysed in mouth); lysozyme acts antibacterial.

sections.heading: 3. Pharynx & oesophagus
sections.html: The pharynx is the common passage for food and air; the glottis (respiratory) and gullet (oesophageal opening) are guarded during swallowing. The oesophagus conducts food to the stomach by peristalsis. No digestion occurs here.

sections.heading: 4. Stomach & gastric digestion
sections.html: J-shaped expandable organ. Gastric glands secrete HCl, pepsinogen, mucus, intrinsic factor. Parietal (oxyntic) cells → HCl; chief (peptic) cells → pepsinogen (activated to pepsin by HCl). HCl kills bacteria, acidifies food, activates pepsin. Mucus and bicarbonate protect the mucosa from concentrated HCl. Gastrin stimulates gastric secretion; enterogastrone inhibits it when chyme enters duodenum.

sections.heading: 5. Liver, gall bladder & bile
sections.html: The liver is the largest gland; hepatic cells secrete bile stored in the gall bladder. Bile has bile salts, bile pigments (bilirubin/biliverdin — give yellow colour to stools in breast-fed infants) and no digestive enzymes. Bile emulsifies fats (increases surface area for lipase action) and neutralises acidic chyme. Bile juice is essential for fat digestion.

sections.heading: 6. Pancreas & pancreatic juice
sections.html: Exocrine pancreas secretes pancreatic juice into the duodenum via the pancreatic duct. Contains trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase, pancreatic amylase, lipase, nucleases. Enterokinase of intestinal juice activates trypsinogen → trypsin (which activates other zymogens). Pancreatic juice is alkaline (HCO₃⁻).

sections.heading: 7. Small intestine — structure
sections.html: Longest part of the alimentary canal (duodenum, jejunum, ileum). Inner surface has circular folds, villi and microvilli to increase absorption area. Crypts of Lieberkühn (simple tubular glands) secrete intestinal juice. Brunner's glands (duodenum) secrete alkaline mucus. The ileum is the main site of absorption and completion of digestion.

sections.heading: 8. Succus entericus (intestinal juice)
sections.html: Succus entericus contains many enzymes: enterokinase, aminopeptidases, dipeptidases, maltase, lactase, sucrase, lipase, nucleotidases. Carboxypeptidase requires zinc. Final digestion of peptides, disaccharides and nucleotides occurs here. Nucleases are present in pancreatic juice, not typically listed as absent from succus entericus in the same way.

sections.heading: 9. Digestion of biomolecules
sections.html:
• Carbohydrates: starch → maltose (salivary & pancreatic amylase) → glucose (disaccharidases).
  • Proteins: pepsin in stomach → peptides; trypsin/chymotrypsin in intestine → smaller peptides → amino acids (peptidases).
  • Fats: emulsified by bile → digested by lipase to fatty acids + monoglycerides.
  • Nucleic acids: pancreatic nucleases → nucleotides → nucleosides/nitrogenous bases.

sections.heading: 10. Absorption & transport
sections.html: Absorption — end products pass through intestinal mucosa into blood/lymph. Monosaccharides, amino acids, Na⁺ and other electrolytes via active transport; fatty acids and glycerol → chylomicrons → lymph (lacteals). Water moves by osmosis following solute absorption. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) with fats; water-soluble via blood. Vitamin B₁₂ richest in liver/Spirulina; some B vitamins synthesised by gut bacteria.

sections.heading: 11. Large intestine & egestion
sections.html: Colon reabsorbs water and electrolytes; hosts beneficial bacteria (vitamin synthesis, gas production). Faeces consist of undigested residue, bacteria, bile pigments. Appendix is a vestigial lymphoid organ. Parasites of intestine include tapeworm, roundworm, pinworm.

chapters.title: Reproduction in Organisms
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Unit VI Chapter 1: why organisms reproduce, life spans, asexual modes (fission, budding, fragmentation, spores, vegetative propagation) and the essentials of sexual reproduction — meiosis, gametes, fertilisation, zygote formation, and reproductive strategies in plants and animals.

sections.heading: 1. Reproduction — why and how
sections.html: Reproduction enables continuity of the species by producing progeny similar to parents. It is not a defining property of life (many organisms do not reproduce yet are living), but it is essential for species survival. Organisms reproduce by asexual (single parent, no gamete fusion) or sexual (two parents/gametes fuse) methods. Juvenile phase precedes reproductive maturity; senescence follows. Reproductive events are seasonal in many plants and animals (photoperiod-sensitive breeders).

sections.heading: 2. Life span
sections.html: Every organism has a characteristic life span — the period from birth to natural death. It varies enormously: bacteria minutes to hours; insects days to weeks; rice ~1 year; butterfly ~1–2 weeks; crow ~15 years; dog ~10–13 years; cat ~15–20 years; elephant ~60–90 years; tortoise ~100–150 years; peepal/Banyan tree hundreds of years. Life span is not correlated with body size.

sections.heading: 3. Asexual reproduction
sections.html:
Asexual reproduction — offspring from a single parent without meiosis/fertilisation; progeny are genetically identical (clones). Common modes:

  • Binary fission — Amoeba, bacteria, Paramoecium (parent divides into two).
  • Budding — yeast, Hydra, sponges (outgrowth detaches).
  • Fragmentation — fungi, filamentous algae, protonema of mosses.
  • Spores — Zoospores (motile, flagellated, in Chlamydomonas); conidia (Penicillium); gemmules (sponges); bulbils (Agave).

In unicellular organisms growth and reproduction are synonymous. Asexual reproduction is fast and simple but produces little variation.

sections.heading: 4. Vegetative propagation
sections.html:
Vegetative propagation in plants — new plants from vegetative parts (asexual, used in horticulture):

  • Rhizome — banana, ginger, turmeric.
  • Tuber — potato (eyes = buds).
  • Bulb — onion, garlic.
  • Offset — water hyacinth (Eichhornia).
  • Runner/stolon — grass, strawberry (not water hyacinth).
  • Adventitious buds — notches on Bryophyllum leaves; bulbils on Agave.

Water hyacinth ('Terror of Bengal') — fastest-spreading aquatic weed; clogs water bodies, kills fish by deoxygenation. Parthenocarpic fruits (e.g. banana) develop without fertilisation.

sections.heading: 5. Sexual reproduction — events & meiosis
sections.html:
Sexual reproduction involves: (i) pre-fertilisation (gametogenesis), (ii) fertilisation/syngamy (fusion of gametes → zygote), (iii) post-fertilisation (embryogenesis). Gametes are usually haploid; formed from diploid meiocytes by meiosis (reduces chromosome number by half). Syngamy restores diploidy in the zygote. The most critical event is fertilisation. Offspring show more variation than asexual progeny because gametes from two parents combine qualitatively different genetic material.

Haploid parental body: most fungi and some algae (e.g. Volvox, Chlamydomonas). Diploid dominant: gymnosperms, angiosperms, most animals. Ophioglossum (a fern) has the highest chromosome number among plants tested in NEET contexts.

sections.heading: 6. Fertilisation strategies in animals
sections.html: External fertilisation — gametes released in water; needs moist environment (most fishes, amphibians). Internal fertilisation — fusion inside the female body (reptiles, birds, mammals); associated with oviparity (egg-laying: reptiles, birds), viviparity (live birth: most mammals including humans), or ovoviviparity (egg retained in body: some sharks, lizards). Oviparous examples: frog, lizard, bird; viviparous: human, cow, dog, horse, whale. Humans are continuous breeders (reproductively active throughout adult life).

sections.heading: 7. Sexual reproduction in plants — special cases
sections.html:
• Monoecious — male and female flowers on same plant (cucurbits, coconut, castor, maize); prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy.
  • Dioecious — male and female on separate plants (papaya, date palm, cannabis); prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.
  • Bamboo — gregarious flowering once in 12–120 years, then dies.
  • Strobilanthus kunthiana (Neelakurinji) — flowers once in 12 years.
  • In bryophytes and pteridophytes male gametes are motile and need water for transfer.
  • Chara — oogonium (female) upper, antheridium (male) lower on same plant.
  • After fertilisation in angiosperms: ovule → seed; ovary → fruit (pericarp); integuments → seed coat (not pericarp).

chapters.title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 1 (Unit VI): flower structure, microsporogenesis and megasporogenesis, pollination and its agents, pollen–pistil interaction, double fertilisation, post-fertilisation development of endosperm, embryo, seed and fruit, and apomixis/polyembryony.

sections.heading: 1. Flower — seat of sexual reproduction
sections.html: All flowering plants (angiosperms) reproduce sexually. The flower bears androecium (stamens = male) and gynoecium (pistil = female). Flowers convey human sentiments (love, grief, etc.) and have ornamental/social value (floriculture). Male gametophyte develops in the pollen grain; female gametophyte in the embryo sac inside the ovule.

sections.heading: 2. Stamen, anther & pollen grain
sections.html:
A stamen = filament + anther. Typical anther is bilobed, dithecous, tetrasporangiate (4 microsporangia). Wall layers: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum (innermost; nourishes pollen; often binucleate). Microsporogenesis: PMC → meiosis → microspore tetrad → pollen grains.

Pollen grain (male gametophyte): exine (sporopollenin, resistant; germ pores) + intine (cellulose/pectin). At shedding: 2-celled (vegetative + generative) in >60% species, or 3-celled (vegetative + 2 male gametes). Rice pollen viable ~30 min; some Rosaceae/Leguminosae months. Stored in liquid N₂ as pollen banks. Parthenium causes pollen allergy. Pollen is rich in nutrients (supplements).

sections.heading: 3. Pistil, ovule & embryo sac
sections.html:
Pistil = stigma + style + ovary. Ovary has locule/placenta bearing ovules. Ovule: funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus, embryo sac. Megasporogenesis: MMC → meiosis → 4 megaspores; usually monosporic (one functional). Embryo sac development: free nuclear divisions → 8-nucleate, 7-celled at maturity:

  • Egg apparatus (micropylar): 2 synergids (with filiform apparatus) + 1 egg.
  • Antipodals (3) at chalaza.
  • Central cell with 2 polar nuclei.

sections.heading: 4. Pollination — types & agents
sections.html:
Pollination = transfer of pollen from anther to stigma.

  • Autogamy — same flower. Cleistogamous flowers (Viola, Oxalis, Commelina) never open; assured self-pollination.
  • Geitonogamy — another flower, same plant (genetically like autogamy).
  • Xenogamy — different plant; only true cross-pollination.

Agents: wind (anemophily — coconut, maize, grass; light non-sticky pollen, feathery stigma), water (hydrophily — Vallisneria, Hydrilla, Zostera; ~30 genera), animals (entomophily — large, colourful, fragrant, nectar; cucumber needs insects). Emasculation + bagging for artificial hybridisation of bisexual flowers.

sections.heading: 5. Outbreeding devices & self-incompatibility
sections.html: To avoid inbreeding depression, plants evolved: (i) pollen release and stigma receptivity not synchronised; (ii) anther and stigma at different positions; (iii) self-incompatibility (genetic — inhibits pollen germination/tube growth); (iv) unisexual flowers (monoecious or dioecious). Unisexuality prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy; dioecy prevents both. Emasculation not needed in unisexual female flowers.

sections.heading: 6. Pollen–pistil interaction
sections.html: Stigma recognises compatible vs incompatible pollen (chemical dialogue). Compatible pollen germinates on stigma → pollen tube grows through style → enters ovule via micropyle → penetrates a synergid via filiform apparatus. If pollen shed at 2-celled stage, generative cell divides in the tube. Events from pollen deposition to tube entry = pollen–pistil interaction. Rejection illustrates self-/interspecific incompatibility.

sections.heading: 7. Double fertilisation
sections.html:
Unique to angiosperms. Two fusions in embryo sac:

  • Syngamy — one male gamete + egg → diploid zygote.
  • Triple fusion — other male gamete + 2 polar nuclei → triploid PEN (primary endosperm nucleus).

PEN → primary endosperm cell → endosperm; zygote → embryo. Double fertilisation = syngamy + triple fusion.

sections.heading: 8. Post-fertilisation — endosperm, embryo, seed & fruit
sections.html:
Endosperm develops before embryo (nutrition). Free-nuclear endosperm → cellular; tender coconut water = free-nuclear endosperm; white kernel = cellular. Non-albuminous (pea, groundnut — endosperm used up) vs albuminous (wheat, maize, castor — persistent endosperm/perisperm).

Embryo: proembryo → globular → heart-shaped → mature. Dicot: epicotyl (plumule), hypocotyl, radicle, 2 cotyledons. Monocot grass: scutellum, coleoptile, coleorhiza.

Seed = fertilised ovule (testa/tegmen from integuments; micropyle pore). Fruit = mature ovary (pericarp). False fruits (apple, strawberry — thalamus contributes). Parthenocarpic fruits (banana) without fertilisation.

sections.heading: 9. Apomixis & polyembryony
sections.html: Apomixis — seed formation without fertilisation (asexual mimicry; grasses, Asteraceae, Citrus, Mango). Diploid egg or nucellar cells form embryos directly. Polyembryony — >1 embryo per seed (Citrus, Mango — nucellar embryos). Apomictic embryos are clones. Useful for fixing hybrid characters without yearly hybrid seed production.

chapters.title: Human Reproduction
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 2: male and female reproductive systems, gametogenesis, the menstrual cycle, fertilisation and implantation, pregnancy and embryonic development, parturition and lactation.

sections.heading: 1. Overview of human reproduction
sections.html: Humans are sexually reproducing, viviparous mammals. Events: gametogenesis → insemination → fertilisation (ampulla of oviduct) → cleavage → blastocyst → implantation → gestation (~9 months) → parturition → lactation. Spermatogenesis continues in old age; oogenesis ceases at ~50 years (menopause).

sections.heading: 2. Male reproductive system
sections.html: Testes in scrotum (2–2.5°C below body temp). Each testis ~250 testicular lobules with seminiferous tubules (spermatogonia + Sertoli cells) and interstitial Leydig cells (androgens). Ducts: rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra. Accessory glands: seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral (Cowper's) — seminal plasma rich in fructose, calcium, enzymes. Penis with glans and foreskin. LH stimulates Leydig cells; FSH acts on Sertoli cells.

sections.heading: 3. Female reproductive system
sections.html: Ovaries (2–4 cm; cortex + medulla) produce ova and ovarian hormones. Oviducts (10–12 cm): infundibulum with fimbriae → ampulla (fertilisation site) → isthmus. Uterus: perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium (cyclical). Opens to vagina via cervix/cervical canal (birth canal with vagina). External genitalia: mons pubis, labia majora/minora, hymen (unreliable virginity indicator), clitoris (junction of labia minora). Mammary glands: 15–20 lobes, alveoli, lactiferous ducts.

sections.heading: 4. Spermatogenesis & sperm structure
sections.html:
Spermatogonia (diploid, 46 ch.) → mitosis → primary spermatocytes → meiosis I → secondary spermatocytes (23) → meiosis II → spermatids (23) → spermiogenesis → spermatozoa; released by spermiation. Triggered at puberty by ↑GnRH → LH + FSH.

Sperm: head (acrosome with enzymes + haploid nucleus), neck, middle piece (mitochondria for motility), tail. ~200–300 million/ejaculate; fertility needs ≥60% normal morphology, ≥40% motility. Viable up to ~48–72 h in female tract.

sections.heading: 5. Oogenesis & folliculogenesis
sections.html: Oogonia form in fetal ovary; arrest at prophase I as primary oocytes. At birth ~2 million; at puberty ~60,000–80,000 primary follicles. Maturation: primary follicle → secondary → tertiary (antrum; theca interna/externa) → Graafian follicle. Primary oocyte completes meiosis I → secondary oocyte + 1st polar body; meiosis II completes after sperm entry. Ovulation releases secondary oocyte with zona pellucida and corona radiata.

sections.heading: 6. Menstrual cycle
sections.html: In female primates; begins at menarche; ~28/29 days. Phases: (1) Menstrual (3–5 days) — endometrial breakdown if no fertilisation. (2) Follicular/proliferative — follicles grow, estrogen from follicles rebuilds endometrium. (3) Ovulatory (~day 14) — LH surge ruptures Graafian follicle. (4) Luteal/secretory — corpus luteum secretes progesterone (maintains endometrium for implantation). Without fertilisation, corpus luteum degenerates → menstruation. Cycle ceases in pregnancy and at menopause (~50 years).

sections.heading: 7. Fertilisation, cleavage & implantation
sections.html:
Fertilisation in ampulla of oviduct (requires simultaneous transport of sperm and ovum). Sperm binds zona pellucida; acrosome enzymes aid entry; polyspermy block. Secondary oocyte completes meiosis II → ovum; pronuclei fuse → diploid zygote (46). Sex determined by sperm (X or Y); ovum always X.

Cleavage in isthmus: 2 → 4 → 8 … blastomeres; 8–16 cell = morula → blastocyst (trophoblast + inner cell mass). Implantation in endometrium → pregnancy.

sections.heading: 8. Pregnancy & embryonic development
sections.html:
Placenta — chorionic villi + uterine tissue; connected by umbilical cord; exchange of O₂/nutrients/wastes; endocrine organ (hCG, hPL, estrogens, progestogens). Relaxin from ovary in late pregnancy.

Germ layers from inner cell mass: ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm. Timeline: heart ~1 month; limbs by 2 months; organ systems by 12 weeks (1st trimester); first foetal movements ~5th month; eyelids separate ~24 weeks. Gestation ~9 months.

sections.heading: 9. Parturition & lactation
sections.html: Parturition — expulsion of foetus via birth canal (cervix + vagina). Induced by foetal-placental signals → foetal ejection reflex → oxytocin (positive feedback on uterine contractions). Placenta expelled after baby. Lactation — mammary glands produce milk; initial secretion = colostrum (antibodies for newborn immunity). Breast-feeding recommended early months.

chapters.title: Reproductive Health
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 3: WHO definition of reproductive health, India's RCH programmes, population stabilisation, contraceptive methods, MTP, sexually transmitted infections, and infertility with assisted reproductive technologies.

sections.heading: 1. Reproductive health & RCH programmes
sections.html: Reproductive health (WHO) = total well-being in all aspects of reproduction — physical, emotional, behavioural, social. India initiated family planning (1951) and now Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes: awareness (adolescence, safe sex, STDs/AIDS), medical care (pregnancy, delivery, contraception, infertility), statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination. CDRI (Lucknow) developed Saheli (non-steroidal oral contraceptive). WHO = World Health Organization.

sections.heading: 2. Population explosion & birth control goals
sections.html: World population: ~2 billion (1900) → ~6 billion (2000) → 7.2 billion (2011). India: ~350 million (1947) → ~1 billion (2000) → 1.2+ billion (2011); growth rate <2%. Causes: ↓death rate/MMR/IMR, more people in reproductive age. Strategies: Hum Do Hamare Do, raising marriageable age (female 18, male 21), incentives for small families, contraception.

sections.heading: 3. Natural & barrier contraception
sections.html:
Natural/traditional: periodic abstinence (avoid coitus days 10–17, fertile period); coitus interruptus (withdrawal); lactational amenorrhea (effective up to 6 months of intense lactation — suppresses gonadotropins). No side effects but higher failure rates.

Barrier: condoms (Nirodh — male; female condom covers vagina/cervix); diaphragms, cervical caps, vaults + spermicidal jellies. Prevent semen entry; also protect against STIs/AIDS.

sections.heading: 4. IUDs, oral pills & injectables
sections.html:
IUDs (Lippes loop; copper — CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375; hormone — Progestasert, LNG-20): inserted in uterus; ↑phagocytosis of sperm; Cu²⁺ suppresses sperm motility; hormone IUDs make uterus unsuitable for implantation and cervix hostile to sperm. Ideal for spacing/delaying pregnancy.

Oral pills: progestogen or progestogen–estrogen, 21 days + 7-day gap; inhibit ovulation, alter cervical mucus. Saheli — once-a-week, non-steroidal. Injectables/implants (Figure 3.3). Emergency contraception within 72 h of coitus.

sections.heading: 5. Surgical sterilisation
sections.html: Sterilisation — terminal method blocking gamete transport. Vasectomy (male): small part of vas deferens tied/removed via scrotal incision. Tubectomy (female): part of fallopian tube tied/removed. Highly effective; poor reversibility. Does not stop gamete formation.

sections.heading: 6. Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP)
sections.html: MTP — intentional termination before full term; legalised in India 1971. ~45–50 million/year worldwide. Safest in first trimester (≤12 weeks); one registered practitioner's opinion sufficient within 12 weeks; two practitioners for 12–24 weeks (Amendment Act 2017). Misuse of amniocentesis + MTP for female foeticide is illegal. Second trimester abortions riskier.

sections.heading: 7. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
sections.html: STIs/RTIs/VD: Gonorrhoea (Neisseria), Syphilis (Treponema), Genital herpes, Chlamydia, Genital warts (HPV), Trichomoniasis, Hepatitis-B, HIV/AIDS. High incidence in age group 15–24. Prevention: avoid unknown/multiple partners; condoms; early treatment. Hepatitis-B, herpes, HIV not fully curable. Complications: PID, infertility, still birth, ectopic pregnancy. Females often asymptomatic early.

sections.heading: 8. Infertility & assisted reproductive technology (ART)
sections.html:
Infertility — unable to conceive after 2 years of unprotected cohabitation; male and female causes both common. ART:

  • IVF + ET ('test tube baby') — zygote/early embryo (≤8 blastomeres) transferred to uterus (IUT) or ZIFT (zygote to fallopian tube).
  • GIFT — ovum + sperm transferred to fallopian tube (requires functional tubes).
  • ICSI — sperm injected into ovum.
  • AI/IUI — artificial insemination (semen into vagina or uterus).

Legal adoption is also encouraged. Infertility clinics diagnose and treat reproductive disorders.

chapters.title: Principles of Inheritance and Variation
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 4: Mendel's laws, monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, chromosomal theory, linkage, sex determination, mutation, and Mendelian and chromosomal genetic disorders.

sections.heading: 1. Genetics — inheritance & variation
sections.html: Genetics deals with inheritance (transmission of characters from parents to offspring) and variation (differences among progeny). Characters are controlled by genes (Mendel's 'factors') — units of inheritance on chromosomes. Alleles are alternate forms of a gene. Genotype = genetic constitution; phenotype = observable expression.

sections.heading: 2. Mendel's laws & pea experiments
sections.html: Gregor Mendel (1856–1863) studied garden pea (Pisum) with 7 contrasting trait pairs (tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled seeds, yellow/green seeds, etc.) using true-breeding lines and artificial cross-pollination. He applied statistics and proposed: Law of Dominance (one allele masks the other in heterozygote) and Law of Segregation (alleles separate during gamete formation). Rediscovered in 1900 by de Vries, Correns and Tschermak.

sections.heading: 3. Inheritance of one gene
sections.html:
Monohybrid cross (Tt × tt or TT × tt): F₁ all dominant phenotype; F₂ phenotypic ratio 3:1, genotypic 1:2:1. Homozygous (TT, tt) vs heterozygous (Tt). Punnett square (Reginald Punnett) predicts genotypes. Test cross = dominant individual × recessive homozygote to determine genotype.

Incomplete dominance — F₁ intermediate (snapdragon pink RR × rr). Co-dominance — both alleles expressed (AB blood group: IA and IB). Multiple alleles — >2 alleles in population (ABO: IA, IB, i). Dominance depends on gene product and phenotype examined.

sections.heading: 4. Inheritance of two genes & chromosomal theory
sections.html: Dihybrid cross (RRYY × rryy): F₁ RrYy; selfing gives F₂ ratio 9:3:3:1 — Law of Independent Assortment (segregation of one gene pair independent of another). Chromosomal theory (Sutton & Boveri, 1902): genes on chromosomes; chromosome behaviour in meiosis parallels Mendelian segregation. Thomas Hunt Morgan used Drosophila melanogaster to verify the theory.

sections.heading: 5. Linkage & recombination
sections.html: Genes on the same chromosome show linkage (tend to stay together); recombination = non-parental combinations. Morgan's dihybrid crosses on X-linked genes deviated from 9:3:3:1. Tightly linked genes show low recombination (white–yellow 1.3%); loosely linked show more (white–miniature 37.2%). Alfred Sturtevant used recombination frequency to map gene positions.

sections.heading: 6. Polygenic inheritance
sections.html: Polygenic traits — controlled by three or more genes with additive effects; show continuous variation (human height, skin colour). Environment also influences phenotype. Each dominant allele contributes incrementally to the trait.

sections.heading: 7. Pleiotropy
sections.html: Pleiotropy — one gene affects multiple phenotypes (often via metabolic pathways). Example: phenylketonuria (mutation in phenylalanine hydroxylase) → mental retardation + reduced pigmentation.

sections.heading: 8. Sex determination
sections.html:
XO type (grasshopper): males XO, females XX. XY type (humans, Drosophila): males XY, females XX — male heterogamety. ZW type (birds): females ZW, males ZZ — female heterogamety. Human sex determined by sperm (X or Y); 50% probability each pregnancy.

Honey bee — haplodiploid: fertilised egg → female (diploid, 32 ch.); unfertilised → male drone (haploid, 16 ch.) by parthenogenesis. Drones have no father, cannot have sons.

sections.heading: 9. Mutation
sections.html: Mutation — alteration of DNA sequence → genotype/phenotype change. Point mutation — single base pair change (sickle cell: GAG→GUG in β-globin). Chromosomal aberrations — deletion, duplication, insertion; common in cancer. Mutagens: UV radiation, chemicals.

sections.heading: 10. Genetic disorders & pedigree analysis
sections.html:
Pedigree analysis traces inheritance across generations. Mendelian disorders (single gene): haemophilia (X-linked recessive), colour blindness (X-linked recessive), sickle-cell anaemia (autosomal recessive; HbSHbS; Glu→Val at β-6), phenylketonuria (autosomal recessive), thalassemia (α/β globin), cystic fibrosis.

Chromosomal disorders: Down's syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner's (45, X0), Klinefelter's (47, XXY). Aneuploidy = gain/loss of chromosome(s); polyploidy = whole set gain (common in plants).

chapters.title: Molecular Basis of Inheritance
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 5: DNA structure and packaging, the search for genetic material, replication, transcription, genetic code, translation, gene regulation, Human Genome Project and DNA fingerprinting.

sections.heading: 1. Overview — DNA as genetic material
sections.html: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the genetic material in most organisms; RNA in some viruses. Central dogma (Crick): DNA → RNA → Protein. Nucleotides join via 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds; polynucleotide has 5′ and 3′ ends.

sections.heading: 2. DNA structure & packaging
sections.html:
Watson & Crick (1953) double helix: antiparallel strands, A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds), pitch 3.4 nm, ~10 bp/turn. Chargaff's rules: A=T, G=C. Human haploid DNA ~3.3×10⁹ bp; E. coli ~4.6×10⁶ bp.

Packaging: prokaryotes — nucleoid; eukaryotes — histone octamer + DNA = nucleosome ('beads-on-string') → chromatin → chromosomes. Euchromatin (transcriptionally active) vs heterochromatin (inactive). NHC proteins help higher-order coiling.

sections.heading: 3. Search for genetic material
sections.html: Griffith (1928) — S. pneumoniae transformation: heat-killed S (smooth/virulent) + live R (rough) → mice die; 'transforming principle'. Avery, MacLeod & McCarty — DNA causes transformation. Hershey & Chase (1952) — bacteriophage: ³²P-DNA entered bacteria, ³⁵S-protein did not → DNA is genetic material. DNA must replicate, be stable, mutate, and express Mendelian characters.

sections.heading: 4. RNA world
sections.html: RNA was likely the first genetic material — also catalytic (ribozymes). RNA is more reactive (2′-OH); DNA evolved for stable storage (thymine replaces uracil; double-stranded with repair). TMV and QB phage use RNA as genetic material.

sections.heading: 5. DNA replication
sections.html:
Semiconservative (Watson-Crick): each daughter DNA has one parental + one new strand. Proved by Meselson & Stahl (¹⁵N/¹⁴N in E. coli) and Taylor (radioactive thymidine in Vicia faba).

DNA-dependent DNA polymerase synthesises 5′→3′ at replication fork. Leading strand continuous; lagging strand discontinuous (Okazaki fragments, joined by DNA ligase). Requires origin of replication (vectors provide ori for rDNA).

sections.heading: 6. Transcription
sections.html:
Transcription — DNA → RNA (complementarity; A pairs with U). Only one strand (template 3′→5′) copied per transcription unit: promoter – structural gene – terminator. Coding strand (5′→3′) has same sequence as RNA (T for U).

Bacterial RNAs: mRNA, tRNA, rRNA (one RNA polymerase). Eukaryotes: split genes — exons (expressed) + introns (spliced out); monocistronic vs bacterial polycistronic.

sections.heading: 7. Genetic code
sections.html: Genetic code — triplet codons on mRNA specify amino acids. Properties: triplet, unambiguous, degenerate, universal (minor exceptions), non-overlapping, commaless. Start codon AUG (Met); stop codons UAA, UAG, UGA. Deciphered by Nirenberg, Khorana, Ochoa.

sections.heading: 8. Translation
sections.html: Translation — mRNA → protein at ribosomes. tRNA has anticodon; amino acid attached at 3′ end. Initiation, elongation, termination. Ribosome = rRNA + proteins; reads mRNA 5′→3′. Polysome = several ribosomes on one mRNA.

sections.heading: 9. Regulation of gene expression
sections.html: In bacteria, gene expression regulated so proteins are made only when needed. Lac operon (Jacob & Monod) in E. coli: structural genes (z, y, a) for lactose metabolism; operator, promoter, regulator (repressor). Lactose = inducer. Positive and negative regulation. Eukaryotes: transcription factors, enhancers, silencers, chromatin modification.

sections.heading: 10. Human Genome Project
sections.html: HGP — international effort to sequence entire human genome (~3 billion bp). Goals: identify all genes, determine sequences, store in databases, address ethical/legal/social issues. Bioinformatics — analyse sequence data. DNA polymorphism — basis for genetic diversity.

sections.heading: 11. DNA fingerprinting
sections.html: DNA fingerprinting (DNA profiling) — identifies individuals by VNTR or STR repeats (Southern blot / PCR). Applications: forensic science, paternity/maternity disputes, pedigree analysis, wildlife conservation. DNA from blood, hair, saliva, sperm.

chapters.title: Evolution
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 6: origin of life, Darwinian evolution, evidences, adaptive radiation, Hardy-Weinberg principle, geological history of life, and human evolution.

sections.heading: 1. Evolutionary biology — overview
sections.html: Evolution — change in allele frequencies over generations; origin and diversification of life. Evolutionary biology studies history of life on Earth. Earth ~4.5 billion years old; universe ~13.8 billion years.

sections.heading: 2. Origin of life
sections.html:
Big Bang → galaxies → solar system. Early Earth: reducing atmosphere (CH₄, NH₃, water vapour). Panspermia — life from space (rejected as sole explanation). Spontaneous generation disproved by Pasteur.

Oparin & Haldane — chemical evolution preceded life. Miller-Urey (1953) — amino acids from CH₄, H₂, NH₃, H₂O + electric discharge. First self-replicating macromolecules ~3 bya; first cells ~2000 mya.

sections.heading: 3. Theories of evolution — Darwin & Lamarck
sections.html:
Special creation challenged in 19th century. Charles Darwin (HMS Beagle voyage) — gradual evolution, common ancestry, extinctions. Natural selection: variation exists; better-adapted individuals leave more progeny (reproductive fitness). Alfred Wallace independently proposed similar theory.

Lamarck — use and disuse of organs (e.g. giraffe neck); not accepted. de Vries — mutations cause saltation (sudden large change).

sections.heading: 4. Evidences for evolution
sections.html:
Paleontological — fossils in sedimentary rocks; extinct forms (dinosaurs). Comparative anatomy: homologous organs (divergent evolution — whale/bat/human forelimbs) vs analogous (convergent — wings of butterfly and bird). Embryology — von Baer over Haeckel. Biochemical — protein/gene sequence similarities.

Industrial melanism (England): pre-industrial white moths on lichen-covered trees; post-industrial dark moths on sooty trunks — natural selection. Anthropogenic selection — antibiotic/herbicide resistance.

sections.heading: 5. Adaptive radiation
sections.html: Adaptive radiation — rapid evolution of many species from a common ancestor into different habitats. Darwin's finches (Galapagos) — varied beaks from seed-eating ancestor. Australian marsupials — diversified on isolated continent. Convergent evolution — placental wolf vs Tasmanian wolf marsupial.

sections.heading: 6. Biological evolution & fitness
sections.html: Evolution by natural selection in cellular life. Fitness = reproductive success; must have genetic basis. Branching descent + natural selection = Darwinian theory. Variation from mutation, recombination, gene flow, genetic drift.

sections.heading: 7. Mechanism of evolution
sections.html: Natural selection acts on heritable variation. Limited resources → competition → differential survival/reproduction. Speciation when populations diverge. Selection types: stabilising, directional, disruptive. Evolution is stochastic, not directed.

sections.heading: 8. Hardy-Weinberg principle
sections.html: Allele frequencies stable across generations in ideal population: p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (p + q = 1). Genetic equilibrium disturbed by: gene migration/flow, genetic drift, mutation, recombination, natural selection. Founder effect — new population from small group. Genetic drift may cause speciation.

sections.heading: 9. Geological time scale & life's history
sections.html: ~2000 mya first cells; 500 mya invertebrates; 350 mya jawless fish; 320 mya plants on land; lobefins → amphibians; reptiles with amniotic eggs; dinosaurs dominant, extinct ~65 mya; mammals diversified; coelacanth 'living fossil'. Continental drift affected distribution (South American marsupials).

sections.heading: 10. Origin & evolution of man
sections.html: Primates: Dryopithecus (ape-like), Ramapithecus (man-like). ~3–4 mya hominids in Africa. Australopithecus — upright, ~4 ft. Homo habilis (650–800 cc brain). Homo erectus (~900 cc, Java). Neanderthal (1400 cc). Homo sapiens in Africa; ice age 75,000–10,000 ya. Cave art Bhimbetka (MP) ~18,000 ya.

chapters.title: Human Health and Disease
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 7: common infectious diseases, immunity and vaccination, AIDS, cancer, and drug/alcohol/tobacco abuse with prevention strategies.

sections.heading: 1. Health — definition & determinants
sections.html: Health (WHO) = complete physical, mental and social well-being — not merely absence of disease. Affected by genetic disorders, infections and life style (diet, hygiene, exercise, habits). Balanced diet, personal/public hygiene, yoga, vaccination and vector control promote health.

sections.heading: 2. Common diseases in humans
sections.html:
