Typhoid — Salmonella typhi; Widal test; high fever, constipation. Pneumonia — Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae; alveoli fill with fluid. Common cold — rhinoviruses. Malaria — Plasmodium (P. vivax, P. malariae, P. falciparum malignant); Anopheles vector; sporozoites → liver → RBCs → haemozoin → fever cycles.

Amoebiasis — E. histolytica; housefly carrier. Ascariasis — Ascaris; Filariasis/elephantiasis — Wuchereria; mosquito vector. Ringworm — Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton fungi. Prevention: hygiene, safe water, vector control, vaccines (smallpox eradicated).

sections.heading: 3. Immunity
sections.html:
Innate immunity (non-specific): physical (skin, mucus), physiological (stomach acid, tears), cellular (PMNL, macrophages, NK cells), cytokine (interferons).

Acquired immunity (specific, memory): B-lymphocytes → antibodies (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE); humoral response. T-lymphocytes → CMI; graft rejection (self vs non-self). Active immunity — body makes antibodies (vaccination). Passive — ready-made (colostrum IgA, maternal via placenta, antitoxin).

Allergy — IgE, histamine (mast cells). Autoimmunity — rheumatoid arthritis. Lymphoid organs: bone marrow, thymus (primary); spleen, lymph nodes, MALT (secondary).

sections.heading: 4. AIDS
sections.html: AIDS — Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome; caused by HIV (retrovirus, RNA genome, reverse transcriptase). Transmission: sexual contact, contaminated blood, shared needles, mother-to-child via placenta. Not spread by casual touch. HIV destroys helper T-lymphocytes → opportunistic infections. Diagnosis: ELISA. Prevention: NACO/WHO programmes, safe blood, disposable needles, condoms, awareness. No complete cure; antiretroviral drugs prolong life.

sections.heading: 5. Cancer
sections.html: Cancer — uncontrolled cell division; loss of contact inhibition. Benign tumours localised; malignant invade tissues and metastasise via blood. Causes: carcinogens (UV, X-rays, tobacco smoke), oncogenic viruses, proto-oncogenes. Detection: biopsy, histopathology, radiography, CT, MRI. Treatment: surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy (α-interferon).

sections.heading: 6. Drugs, alcohol & tobacco abuse
sections.html:
Opioids — heroin (diacetylmorphine from poppy Papaver somniferum). Cannabinoids — Cannabis sativa (marijuana, hashish, ganja). Cocaine — Erythroxylum coca; blocks dopamine transport. Tobacco — nicotine; cancers of lung, bladder, throat; CO reduces O₂ binding.

Adolescence (12–18 yr) vulnerable — curiosity, peer pressure, academic stress. Addiction vs dependence (withdrawal syndrome). IV drug use → AIDS, Hepatitis B. Doping — anabolic steroids. Prevention: parental support, counselling, early detection, de-addiction programmes.

chapters.title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
chapters.topic: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Unit VI Chapter 9: plant breeding and tissue culture, single cell protein and biofortification, and animal husbandry — dairy, poultry, apiculture, aquaculture and controlled breeding.

sections.heading: 1. Food production — overview
sections.html: With a growing human population, enhancement of food production is essential. Strategies include plant breeding, tissue culture, animal husbandry (dairy, poultry, fisheries, apiculture) and microbial foods (SCP). In India agriculture accounts for ~14% of GDP and employs ~50% of the population. Good breeds should be high-yielding, disease-resistant, tolerant to climatic stress and have better quality products. A shift from grain to meat diet increases cereal demand (~3–10 kg grain per kg meat).

sections.heading: 2. Plant breeding
sections.html: Plant breeding manipulates plant species for superior crops. Steps: (i) collection of germplasm (entire collection of diverse alleles — the gene pool); (ii) evaluation and selection of parents; (iii) hybridization of selected parents; (iv) selection and testing of superior recombinants; (v) testing, release and commercialisation of new cultivars. Emasculation (removal of anthers) and bagging (covering emasculated flower) prevent unwanted pollination in cross-pollinated crops. Self-pollination for several generations yields pure lines. Mutation breeding uses physical/chemical mutagens. The Green Revolution (1960s–70s) — high-yielding, disease-resistant wheat and rice via plant breeding — was led globally by Norman Borlaug and in India by M. S. Swaminathan. Indian varieties: wheat (HL-21, Sonalika, Kalyan Sona); rice (IR-8, Jaya, Ratna); sugarcane (Saccharum barberi × S. officinarum); millets; Pusa varieties (e.g. Pusa Gaurav — mustard; Pusa Komal — cowpea; Pusa Sadabahar — chilli); Himgiri (wheat — leaf/stripe rust resistant).

sections.heading: 3. Tissue culture & micropropagation
sections.html: Tissue culture regenerates whole plants from explants on nutrient medium under aseptic conditions. Totipotency — capacity of a cell to generate a whole plant. Micropropagation (clonal propagation) produces thousands of identical plants from shoot tips/meristems — virus-free plants (e.g. banana, potato, sugarcane). Steps: explant → callus → shoot/root induction → hardening → field transfer. Somaclonal variation — genetic variation among tissue-culture-derived plants. Anther culture → haploid plants; embryo rescue saves weak interspecific hybrids; protoplast fusion → somatic hybrids (e.g. Pomato = potato + tomato). Cryopreservation stores germplasm at −196 °C (liquid N₂). Hormones: auxin + cytokinin ratio controls organogenesis.

sections.heading: 4. Heterosis & hybrid seeds
sections.html: Heterosis (hybrid vigour) — superior performance of F₁ hybrids over parents in yield, growth, uniformity and disease resistance. Commercial hybrid seed production: develop inbred lines by repeated self-pollination → cross two inbreds → single cross hybrid; double cross and triple cross hybrids use more parental lines for greater vigour but lower uniformity. Hybrid seeds must be purchased each season (F₂ segregates). Examples: maize, rice, sorghum hybrid varieties (e.g. P-1542).

sections.heading: 5. Biofortification
sections.html: Biofortification breeds crops with higher levels of vitamins, minerals, proteins or healthier oils — sustainable remedy for hidden hunger (micronutrient deficiency: iron, vitamin A, iodine, zinc). Targets: protein quality (lysine, tryptophan in maize/wheat); micronutrients (iron, vitamin A); oil quality. Examples: Atlas 66 (wheat, high protein); Golden rice (β-carotene / vitamin A precursor); iron-rich varieties. Distinct from fortification (adding nutrients during processing).

sections.heading: 6. Single cell protein (SCP)
sections.html: Single cell protein (SCP) — microbial biomass (bacteria, yeasts, algae, filamentous fungi) grown on industrial/agricultural waste, harvested and used as food/rich protein supplement. Advantages: rapid biomass production, independent of land, uses waste substrates. Sources: Spirulina (alga, 60% protein, on wastewater); Methylophilus methylotrophus (bacterium, 43% protein, on methanol); Fusarium (fungus, Pruteen, on glucose); Candida utilis (yeast, on molasses). SCP can reduce pressure on agricultural land for protein.

sections.heading: 7. Animal breeding & husbandry
sections.html: Animal husbandry — care and breeding of livestock (cattle, sheep, goat, poultry, pig) for food, fibre and labour. Breeding aims: increased milk/meat/egg production, disease resistance, quality. Methods: inbreeding (closely related animals — exposes harmful recessives, reduces fertility; used to develop pure lines); outbreeding — out-crossing (same breed, unrelated), cross-breeding (superior breeds, e.g. Hissardale = Bikaneri × Marino sheep), interspecific hybridization (mule = horse × donkey, sterile). MOET (Multiple Ovulation Embryo Transfer): FSH → superovulation → AI → non-surgical recovery at 8-cell stage → embryo transfer to surrogates — rapid multiplication of elite cows. Artificial insemination (AI) uses proven sire semen. Castrated bull → docile bullock for farm work.

sections.heading: 8. Apiculture (bee-keeping)
sections.html: Apiculture — maintenance of honeybee hives for honey and wax. Species: Apis indica (common Indian), A. dorsata (rock bee), A. florae (little bee), A. mellifera (Italian, high yield). Products: honey (fructose/glucose, minerals, enzymes), bee wax, propolis, royal jelly. Bee-keeping needs: knowledge of nature/habits of bees, suitable location, catching/swarming, management during flowering. Hives in crop fields during flowering increase pollination and crop yield. Worker bees live ~6 weeks (busy season) to months (winter).

sections.heading: 9. Fisheries & aquaculture
sections.html: Fisheries — industry dealing with catching, processing and selling fish/shellfish. Aquaculture (pisciculture) — rearing fish in confined water bodies. Freshwater fishes: Catla (surface feeder), Rohu (column feeder), Mrigal (bottom feeder), common carp, grass carp, silver carp. Marine: Hilsa, pomfret, mackerel. Composite fish culture stocks 5–6 compatible species with different feeding niches for high yield without competition. Prawn/fish culture integrated with rice paddies in some systems. Common carp introduced to India by foreigners.

sections.heading: 10. Dairy & poultry management
sections.html: Dairy farm management — processes for improved milk yield and quality: selection of high-yielding milch breeds (Sahiwal, Red Sindhi — indigenous; Holstein-Friesian, Jersey — exotic; cross-breeds for hybrid vigour), proper housing, feeding, hygiene, veterinary care, AI with superior bulls, record-keeping. Poultry — domesticated fowl for eggs and meat. Broilers (meat, fast growth) and layers (egg production). Breeds: Leghorn, Rhode Island Red, Aseel (Aisha). Management: breed selection, disease-free stock, balanced feed, hygiene, temperature control. Infected birds culled; bird flu not transmitted by properly cooked chicken/eggs (>100 °C).

chapters.title: Microbes in Human Welfare
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 8: useful microbes in household products, industrial fermentations, sewage treatment, biogas, biocontrol agents and biofertilisers.

sections.heading: 1. Microbes — diversity & overview
sections.html: Microbes (bacteria, fungi, protozoa, viruses, viroids, prions) are ubiquitous — soil, water, air, thermal vents, deep soil, snow. Prions are proteinaceous infectious agents. Bacteria and fungi grow on nutritive media as visible colonies. Most microbes are useful; some cause disease (Ch. 7). This chapter covers household, industrial, environmental and agricultural applications.

sections.heading: 2. Microbes in household products
sections.html: Curd — Lactobacillus (LAB) ferments milk → lactic acid coagulates proteins; improves vitamin B₁₂; LAB in stomach check pathogens. Dosa/idli/bread — bacterial/yeast fermentation; CO₂ puffs dough (Saccharomyces cerevisiae = baker's/brewer's yeast). Toddy — palm sap fermentation. Cheese — microbes give texture/flavour (Propionibacterium shermanii → CO₂ holes in Swiss cheese; fungi ripen Roquefort).

sections.heading: 3. Microbes in industrial products
sections.html: Large-scale production in fermentors. Beverages — S. cerevisiae ferments malted cereals/fruit juices → ethanol; wine/beer without distillation; whisky/brandy/rum with distillation. Antibiotics — chemical substances from microbes killing/inhibiting other microbes (anti + bio); Penicillin — Fleming (Penicillium notatum); Chain & Florey (Nobel 1945); treated WW-II wounds. Organic acids: citric (Aspergillus niger), acetic (Acetobacter aceti), butyric (Clostridium butylicum), lactic (Lactobacillus). Enzymes/bioactives: lipases (detergents), pectinases/proteases (juice clarification), streptokinase (clot buster), cyclosporin A (Trichoderma polysporum — immunosuppressant), statins (Monascus purpureus — cholesterol lowering).

sections.heading: 4. Microbes in sewage treatment
sections.html: Sewage = municipal wastewater with organic matter and pathogens. Primary treatment — filtration + sedimentation → primary sludge + effluent. Secondary (biological) treatment — aerobic microbes in aeration tanks form flocs, consume organic matter → ↓BOD (biochemical oxygen demand = O₂ needed to oxidise organic matter in 1 L water). Effluent → settling tank → activated sludge (part recycled as inoculum). Remaining sludge → anaerobic digesters → biogas (CH₄, H₂S, CO₂). Ganga/Yamuna Action Plans — more STPs. Untreated sewage pollutes rivers.

sections.heading: 5. Microbes in biogas production
sections.html: Biogas — predominantly methane from anaerobic microbial degradation. Methanogens (e.g. Methanobacterium) on cellulosic material in anaerobic sludge and cattle rumen (break cellulose; humans cannot digest cellulose). Gobar gas plant — cattle dung slurry in concrete tank; floating cover rises with gas; spent slurry = fertiliser. Developed by IARI and KVIC.

sections.heading: 6. Microbes as biocontrol agents
sections.html: Biocontrol — biological control of pests/diseases; reduces toxic pesticides. Organic farming maintains predator–prey balance. Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) — dried spores sprayed; toxin activated in alkaline insect gut → pores in midgut → death; Bt-cotton has Bt toxin genes. Trichoderma — free-living fungus, biocontrol of plant pathogens. Baculoviruses (Nucleopolyhedrovirus) — species-specific insecticides, safe for plants/mammals/birds/fish/non-target insects; useful in IPM. Ladybird (aphids), dragonflies (mosquitoes).

sections.heading: 7. Microbes as biofertilisers
sections.html: Biofertilisers enrich soil nutrients organically. Rhizobium — nodules on legume roots fix N₂. Azospirillum, Azotobacter — free-living N-fixers. Mycorrhiza (Glomus) — fungus aids P uptake; resistance to pathogens, salinity, drought. Cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria) — N-fixation in paddy fields; add organic matter. Commercial biofertilisers reduce chemical fertiliser dependence.

chapters.title: Biotechnology: Principles and Processes
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 9: genetic engineering and bioprocess engineering — restriction enzymes, vectors, host transformation, PCR, rDNA construction, bioreactors and downstream processing.

sections.heading: 1. Principles of biotechnology
sections.html: Biotechnology — use of live organisms/enzymes for useful products. Modern biotech rests on (i) genetic engineering (alter DNA/RNA, change phenotype) and (ii) bioprocess engineering (sterile large-scale manufacture). Alien DNA needs origin of replication (ori) to multiply — cloning. First rDNA: Cohen & Boyer (1972) — antibiotic resistance gene + Salmonella plasmid → E. coli. Three steps: identify DNA, introduce into host, maintain/transfer to progeny.

sections.heading: 2. Restriction enzymes & gel electrophoresis
sections.html: Restriction endonucleases ('molecular scissors') cut DNA at specific recognition sequences (often palindromes, e.g. 5′-GAATTC-3′ for EcoRI). Naming: genus + species + strain + order (EcoRI from E. coli RY13). Sticky ends facilitate ligation. Exonucleases cut ends; endonucleases cut within. Fragments separated by agarose gel electrophoresis (DNA → anode); stained with ethidium bromide under UV; bands eluted for cloning.

sections.heading: 3. Cloning vectors
sections.html: Plasmids and bacteriophages replicate independently. Vector features: (i) ori — copy number control; (ii) selectable marker — antibiotic resistance (ampR, tetR, kanR, chloramphenicol) to identify transformants; (iii) cloning sites — preferably single restriction site (e.g. pBR322 — insertional inactivation of tetR, transformants grow on ampicillin not tetracycline); β-galactosidase insertional inactivation — blue/white colony selection. Plant vectors: modified Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens; animal: disarmed retroviruses.

sections.heading: 4. Competent host & gene delivery
sections.html: DNA is hydrophilic — needs delivery methods. Transformation — E. coli made competent with Ca²⁺, ice → 42 °C heat shock → ice. Alternatives: microinjection (animal nucleus), biolistics/gene gun (plant cells — gold/tungsten particles), disarmed pathogen vectors (Agrobacterium, retrovirus).

sections.heading: 5. rDNA technology steps
sections.html: Sequence: isolate DNA (lysozyme/cellulase/chitinase; RNase, protease; ethanol precipitation) → restrict → isolate fragment → DNA ligase ligation → transfer to host → culture → extract product. PCR — denaturation, primer annealing, extension with Taq polymerase (Thermus aquaticus, thermostable); amplifies DNA in vitro. Selection via selectable markers on transformants.

sections.heading: 6. Bioreactors & downstream processing
sections.html: Recombinant protein from heterologous host. Large-scale: bioreactors (100–1000 L) with agitator, O₂ delivery, foam/pH/temperature control, sampling ports; sparged stirred-tank types. Continuous culture maintains log phase for higher yield. Downstream processing — separation, purification, formulation, preservatives, clinical trials, quality control after biosynthetic stage.

chapters.title: Biotechnology and its Applications
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 10: GM crops, RNAi, recombinant therapeutics, gene therapy, molecular diagnosis, transgenic animals, and ethical/regulatory issues including biopiracy.

sections.heading: 1. Biotechnology applications — overview
sections.html: Biotech applications: therapeutics, diagnostics, GM agriculture, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment, energy. Three research areas: improved catalyst (microbe/enzyme), optimal engineering conditions, downstream purification.

sections.heading: 2. Applications in agriculture
sections.html:
Food options: agrochemical, organic, or GM crop agriculture. Tissue culture — totipotency; micropropagation → somaclones; virus-free plants from meristem; somatic hybridisation (protoplast fusion). GMO/GM plants — abiotic stress tolerance, pest resistance, ↓post-harvest loss, ↑mineral efficiency, enhanced nutrition (Golden Rice — vit A).

Bt cotton — Bacillus thuringiensis cry genes (cryIAc, cryIIAb for bollworms; cryIAb for corn borer); protoxin activated in alkaline insect gut. RNAi — dsRNA silences specific mRNA; used against nematode Meloidegyne incognitia in tobacco via Agrobacterium vectors (sense + antisense RNA).

sections.heading: 3. Applications in medicine
sections.html: Genetically engineered insulin — Eli Lilly (1983): separate A and B chain genes in E. coli, combined by disulphide bonds; identical to human insulin; not orally active (digested). Earlier from cattle/pig pancreas caused allergy. Gene therapy — insert functional genes; first clinical case 1990 — ADA deficiency (adenosine deaminase); lymphocyte culture + retroviral ADA cDNA; permanent cure needs early embryonic gene transfer. Molecular diagnosis — PCR (HIV, cancer mutations), ELISA (antigen–antibody), probe hybridisation/autoradiography.

sections.heading: 4. Transgenic animals
sections.html: Transgenic animals — extra foreign gene expressed. Uses: study gene regulation/development; disease models (cancer, cystic fibrosis, Alzheimer's); biological products (Rosie cow — human α-lactalbumin milk; α-1-antitrypsin for emphysema); vaccine safety testing (polio in mice); toxicity/safety testing. >95% transgenic animals are mice.

sections.heading: 5. Ethical issues & biopiracy
sections.html: GM organisms need regulation — GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee, India). Biopiracy — unauthorised use of bio-resources/traditional knowledge (Basmati rice US patent 1997; turmeric, neem patent attempts). Indian Patents Bill amendments address traditional knowledge. Ethical concerns: unpredictable ecosystem effects, patent equity between developed (rich, low biodiversity) and developing (biodiversity-rich) nations. Rio Convention on Biological Diversity (1992); Johannesburg Summit 2002.

chapters.title: Organisms and Populations
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 11: ecology at organism and population levels — abiotic adaptations, population attributes, growth models, and interspecific interactions.

sections.heading: 1. Ecology — organisms & populations
sections.html: Ecology studies interactions among organisms and with the abiotic environment at levels: organisms, populations, communities, biomes. A population = individuals of a species in a defined area sharing resources and potentially interbreeding. Natural selection operates at population level.

sections.heading: 2. Organism & abiotic factors
sections.html: Organisms respond to temperature, water, light, soil. Homeostasis — steady internal environment. Conformers vs regulators (e.g. birds/mammals thermoregulate). Eurythermal/stenothermal (temperature); euryhaline/stenohaline (salinity). Aestivation (summer) and hibernation (winter) avoid stress. Migration — long-distance movement. Altitude sickness — low O₂, nausea, fatigue. Desert plants: sunken stomata, thick cuticle, C₄/CAM pathways; kangaroo rat meets water needs through internal fat oxidation.

sections.heading: 3. Population attributes
sections.html: Population-level attributes: birth rate, death rate, sex ratio, age distribution. Age pyramid shape → growing/stable/declining population. Population density (N) — numbers, biomass or % cover (banyan vs Parthenium). Indirect measures: fish per trap, pug marks, fecal pellets.

sections.heading: 4. Population growth
sections.html: Density change: Nt+1 = Nt + [(B+I)−(D+E)]. Exponential growth (unlimited resources): dN/dt = rN; Nt = N₀ert; intrinsic rate of natural increase (r); J-shaped curve. Logistic growth: dN/dt = rN((K−N)/K); carrying capacity (K); sigmoid curve; more realistic. Life history — semelparity (bamboo, salmon) vs iteroparity; many small vs few large offspring.

sections.heading: 5. Interspecific interactions
sections.html: Mutualism (+/+) — lichens, mycorrhiza, fig–wasp, orchid–bee pollination. Competition (−/−) — Gause's competitive exclusion (resources limiting); resource partitioning (warblers); competitive release; interference competition. Predation (+/−) — energy transfer, prey regulation, biological control; prickly pear–moth (Australia); predator prudence; prey defences (camouflage, toxins, Monarch butterfly). Parasitism (+/−) — host-specific coevolution; ectoparasites (lice, ticks, Cuscuta) vs endoparasites; brood parasitism (cuckoo/koel). Commensalism (+/0) — orchid on mango, cattle egret. Amensalism (−/0).

chapters.title: Ecosystem
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 12: ecosystem structure and function — productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling, ecological pyramids and succession.

sections.heading: 1. Ecosystem — structure & function
sections.html: An ecosystem = biotic + abiotic components functioning as a unit. Types: terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert) and aquatic (pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary). Components: species composition, stratification. Four functional aspects: productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling. Pond example: phytoplankton producers, zooplankton consumers, fungi/bacteria decomposers.

sections.heading: 2. Productivity
sections.html: Primary production — biomass/organic matter per unit area/time by plants. GPP (gross) − R (respiration) = NPP (net, available to heterotrophs). Secondary productivity — new organic matter by consumers. Global NPP ≈ 170 billion tons; oceans 55 billion (70% area but lower productivity — light/nutrient limitation).

sections.heading: 3. Decomposition
sections.html: Detritus (dead leaves, bark, faeces) → decomposers (bacteria, fungi). Steps: fragmentation (detritivores/earthworms), leaching, catabolism, humification (humus — colloidal, slow decomposition, nutrient reservoir), mineralisation. Rate depends on detritus chemistry (lignin/chitin slow; N/sugars fast) and climate (warm moist favours decomposition).

sections.heading: 4. Energy flow & food chains
sections.html: Sun → <50% PAR; plants capture 2–10% PAR. Unidirectional energy flow. Grazing food chain (GFC): producers → herbivores → carnivores. Detritus food chain (DFC): dead organic matter → decomposers (saprotrophs); major route in terrestrial ecosystems. Food web — interconnected chains. Trophic levels; standing crop (biomass/numbers per unit area). 10% law — ~10% energy transferred between trophic levels; limits GFC length.

sections.heading: 5. Ecological pyramids
sections.html: Pyramids of number, biomass, energy (producers at base, top consumers at apex). Usually upright on land; inverted biomass pyramid in sea (phytoplankton < zooplankton biomass). Energy pyramid always upright — energy lost as heat at each step. Limitations: no omnivory/multiple trophic levels; ignores saprophytes; single-chain assumption.

sections.heading: 6. Ecological succession
sections.html: Succession — orderly sequential change in species composition in a given area. Primary succession — bare/inorganic substrate (new lava, rocks). Secondary succession — previously colonised but disturbed (abandoned farmland). Pioneer species → intermediate → climax community. Hydrarch succession in water → mesic conditions; xerarch on bare rock → forest. Succession leads to stable climax near equilibrium with environment.

chapters.title: Biodiversity and Conservation
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 13: levels and patterns of biodiversity, importance, loss causes, and in situ/ex situ conservation strategies including hotspots and protected areas.

sections.heading: 1. Biodiversity — levels & global patterns
sections.html: Biodiversity (Edward Wilson) = diversity at all biological levels: genetic (Rauvolfia strains, 50,000 rice varieties), species (Western Ghats amphibians), ecological (India's deserts, forests, mangroves). ~1.5 million species described; estimate ~7 million total. >70% animals (70% insects); fungi > vertebrates combined. India: 2.4% land, 8.1% species — one of 12 mega-diversity countries (~45,000 plants, ~90,000 animals recorded).

sections.heading: 2. Patterns of biodiversity
sections.html: Latitudinal gradient — highest diversity in tropics (23.5°N–23.5°S); Colombia 1400 bird spp. vs Greenland 56. Amazon greatest diversity. Reasons: long undisturbed evolution time, less seasonality, more solar energy → productivity. Species–area relationship: log S = log C + Z log A; Z ≈ 0.1–0.2 (regional), 0.6–1.2 (continents). Rivet popper hypothesis (Paul Ehrlich) — species loss erodes ecosystem function like removing rivets from an aircraft.

sections.heading: 3. Importance of species diversity
sections.html: Rich biodiversity → stable, productive, invasion-resistant ecosystems (Tilman's experiments). Why conserve? Narrowly utilitarian (food, drugs — 25% market drugs plant-derived), broadly utilitarian (ecosystem services: Amazon 20% O₂, pollination), ethical (intrinsic value). Sixth extinction — 100–1000× pre-human rates; human-driven.

sections.heading: 4. Loss of biodiversity
sections.html: Evil Quartet causes: (i) habitat loss & fragmentation (tropical rainforests 14%→6%); (ii) over-exploitation (Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon); (iii) alien species invasions (Nile perch in Lake Victoria, Parthenium, Lantana, water hyacinth, African catfish Clarias gariepinus); (iv) co-extinctions. IUCN Red List: 15,500+ threatened; amphibians especially vulnerable. Five past mass extinctions; current rates unprecedented.

sections.heading: 5. Biodiversity conservation
sections.html: In situ — conserve whole ecosystem (save forest to save tiger). Biodiversity hotspots — 34 worldwide (<2% land, high endemism); India: Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Himalaya, Indo-Burma. Protected: 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks, 448 sanctuaries; sacred groves (Meghalaya, Rajasthan, MP). Ex situ — zoos, botanical gardens, cryopreservation, IVF, tissue culture, seed banks. Rio Earth Summit 1992 (CBD); Johannesburg 2002 pledge to reduce biodiversity loss by 2010.

chapters.title: Environmental Issues
chapters.intro: NCERT Class XII Chapter 16: air and water pollution, solid waste, agrochemical effects, radiation, global warming, ozone depletion, deforestation and control measures.

sections.heading: 1. Pollution — overview
sections.html: Pollution — undesirable change in physical, chemical or biological characteristics of air, land or water harming life. Control requires understanding causes and effects. Major issues: air, water, soil, noise, radiation; linked to industrialisation and population growth.

sections.heading: 2. Air pollution & acid rain
sections.html: Air pollutants: CO, CO₂, SO₂, NOx, hydrocarbons, particulates. Automobile exhaust — major source; catalytic converters use Pt-Pd-Rh to convert unburnt hydrocarbons to CO₂/H₂O and CO to CO₂; unleaded petrol required. BS-IV/Bharat Stage emission norms. ESP removes ~99% particulate matter from thermal plant exhaust. Acid rain (pH <5.6) — SO₂/NOx → H₂SO₄/HNO₃; damages monuments, aquatic life. Smog — classical (SO₂+smoke) and photochemical (PAN, acrolein, formaldehyde).

sections.heading: 3. Water pollution & eutrophication
sections.html: BOD measures organic pollution — high BOD = highly polluted water. E. coli indicator of faecal contamination. Eutrophication — nutrient enrichment (nitrates/phosphates from fertilisers) → algal bloom → O₂ depletion → fish kill. Biomagnification — ↑toxicant concentration at successive trophic levels (DDT highest in fish-eating birds). Water hyacinth (Eichhornia) introduced in India chokes water bodies. Arsenic in groundwater (West Bengal). Ganga Action Plan — pollution abatement.

sections.heading: 4. Solid waste & agrochemicals
sections.html: E-waste — discarded computers/electronics; valuable metals (Cu, Fe, Si) but toxic substances (Be, Cd, Hg, Pb); recycling in developing countries hazardous. Sanitary landfills, incineration, composting. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) — biocontrol, pheromones, sterile males; reduces pesticide load. Organic farming — no synthetic chemicals. Green manure, compost, biofertilisers. Rachel Carson — Silent Spring (DDT awareness).

sections.heading: 5. Radioactive waste
sections.html: Nuclear energy — low CO₂ but produces radioactive waste. Disposal: deep underground burial in steel containers lined with concrete; must prevent leakage into biosphere for thousands of years. Radiation causes mutations, cancer; Hiroshima/Nagasaki and Chernobyl effects documented.

sections.heading: 6. Greenhouse effect & global warming
sections.html: Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, CFCs, water vapour) trap outgoing IR radiation → global warming. CO₂ and CH₄ contribute most. Without CO₂, Earth's surface would be ~30 °C colder. Effects: climate change, sea-level rise, glacier melt, species migration/extinction. Kyoto Protocol (1997) — binding emission cuts for developed nations.

sections.heading: 7. Ozone depletion
sections.html: Good ozone in stratosphere (ozonosphere) shields UV-B. Bad ozone in troposphere — pollutant. CFCs (refrigerants, aerosols) release Cl in stratosphere → catalytic ozone destruction. Montreal Protocol (1987) — phase out ozone-depleting substances. Ozone hole over Antarctica. UV-B damages DNA, causes skin cancer, cataracts, immunosuppression.

sections.heading: 8. Deforestation & Chipko
sections.html: Deforestation — conversion of forest to non-forest; causes soil erosion, floods, desertification, ↓biodiversity, climate change. Reforestation restores degraded forests. Chipko Movement (1974) — Garhwal Himalaya; Amrita Devi and villagers hugged trees to prevent felling; inspired eco-feminist forest conservation.
